extraction.body: $6.36 billion moved out of Binance wallets across 10 blockchains in roughly 20 minutes, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, as reported by Reuters. That figure surpasses the 2025 Bybit theft, previously regarded as the largest known cryptocurrency heist on record. Binance estimated its own impact at approximately $6.3 billion and temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while conducting security checks, according to the company's official statement on X. Binance's preliminary investigation identified a potentially compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, though the company later noted additional points of breach. Binance's preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as a likely entry point. Attackers may have used that access to reach a service container, then submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions from there. Binance said it found no evidence that private keys were leaked. Private keys are the cryptographic credentials that directly authorize control over cryptocurrency holdings, so their absence suggests attackers exploited an operational pathway rather than the most direct form of account control. The alleged method raises questions about whether privileged employee devices and associated environments had excessive access to systems capable of authorizing withdrawals at this scale. TRM Labs, Elliptic, and Chainalysis each attributed the attack to North Korea, though those assessments rest on blockchain tracing and pattern analysis rather than a completed criminal indictment. TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , describing it as an elite North Korean hacking unit. The firm said it reached that assessment with high confidence, according to Reuters. Elliptic cited similarities between this fund movement and patterns seen in earlier attacks linked to the same network, according to the Wall Street Journal. Chainalysis also assessed the breach as likely conducted by TraderTraitor, according to CBS News. Those assessments rest on blockchain tracing, infrastructure analysis, and attack-pattern comparison. No public criminal indictment has been filed in connection with this specific incident, and North Korean responsibility should be read as a converging set of private-sector assessments rather than a settled legal finding. The alleged financial motive is consistent with longstanding assessments by U.S. government and international bodies that North Korean cyber operations generate hard currency for a heavily sanctioned state, including programs tied to weapons development. Roughly $3 billion of the affected assets have been frozen on-chain, while the remainder is still being traced across multiple blockchains. Roughly $3 billion of the affected assets have been frozen on-chain through cooperation with blockchain partners, according to Binance's statement. The remaining funds are still being traced, which complicates recovery efforts. Binance said it revoked the affected address authorization and engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners. An updated proof of reserves is planned following remediation. User funds are safe, Binance asserted, though that claim remains unverified pending a full technical post-mortem and updated proof of reserves. User funds are safe, the company stated, and any losses will be covered through its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company reserves. That claim is a company assertion, not an independently verified finding. A completed technical post-mortem and updated proof of reserves have not yet been published. Independent verification of customer-fund status remains pending. The reported entry point raises broader questions about whether large exchanges adequately separate deployment access from financial authorization. The alleged breach path points to a structural question about privilege management at large exchanges. Deployment access and financial authorization are different functions, and the incident raises questions about whether controls separating those functions were sufficient. Binance has not yet published a full technical post-mortem. Until it does, the complete picture of how this happened remains incomplete.

sources.title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’ - The Guardian
passages: The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.
North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered.
The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.
Q&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?
“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit. Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets. Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars. Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003 . “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic. Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist. TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis. An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report. Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.” Teng said Binance had set aside $6.34bn to cover stolen assets. The company was founded by the Chinese-born entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, now a Canadian and United Arab Emirates citizen, who was jailed for four months in 2024 after pleading guilty to money laundering violations. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025. Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks. Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”. In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.” Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. “It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong. North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered. The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic. Binance ⁠is working on the aftermath of the hack with law enforcement ⁠around ⁠the world, ​including the FBI and the US Secret Service. Tether, an issuer of stablecoins, which trade at a value fixed to a conventional currency like the US dollar, said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m. The largest losses related to the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with $3.8bn-worth affected, according to Elliptic. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across almost 150 attacks, according to TRM. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers. Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system. Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident. The UK’s financial watchdogs are monitoring the hack for any potential fallout. While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system. Please share your response in the form below, anonymously if you prefer. We will contact you before we publish any of your submission. If you include other people's names please ask them first. A spokesperson for the FCA said: “While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in the UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.” The Bank of England is also monitoring the hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there are no active concerns. The Bank declined to comment.

Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges.
Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers.
Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach.
Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.

The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”
Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners.

The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.”

extraction.body: Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance . The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers. The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change. In a post on X , Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto. The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains. Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.” Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners. The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.” It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices. Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target , compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee. Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds. Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review. Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.” Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes. Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million . The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction. passages: Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance . The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.
The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change.

In a post on X , Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto.

The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains.
Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”

Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners. The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.”

It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices.

Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target , compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.
Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds.

Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.
Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.”

Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .
According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes.

Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million .

The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction.

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World ​Liberty Financial froze about half ⁠of the stolen assets. The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 ‌billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected ‌to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion. Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more ‌than $1 billion. "We NEVER use any customer funds, so they are not impacted," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said in a post on X. Teng described the breach as a "complex attack" that was not carried out by ⁠one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete traces and evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate." The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said. Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks ​blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring ‌a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea. "TRM attributes the attack to ... North Korea's elite hacking unit," the firm said in an analysis on its website. Both TRM and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible. "This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for ⁠espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts. North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters. The FBI said it was "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private ​partners to understand the scope of ‌the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps." The USSS did not respond to an emailed request for comment. "It's the biggest hack in history," Aravind Srinivasan at market maker GSR said, as crypto prices fell broadly. Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilised. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 6.2% over the past 24 hours at $702, according to CoinMarketCap, while shaky confidence ‌hit listed crypto exchange shares. Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the ⁠crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite ‌and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group. Investor Michael Saylor, among Bitcoin's most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expected Binance to "deliver" on ensuring no customers suffered losses. "Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and ⁠more resilient," he wrote on Friday. coreStoryFacts.text: TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , describing it as an elite North Korean hacking unit.

No public criminal indictment has been filed in connection with this specific incident, and North Korean responsibility should be read as a converging set of private-sector assessments rather than a settled legal finding.

The alleged financial motive is consistent with longstanding assessments by U.S. government and international bodies that North Korean cyber operations generate hard currency for a heavily sanctioned state, including programs tied to weapons development.
Binance's preliminary investigation identified a potentially compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, though the company later noted additional points of breach.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.
North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered.
The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.
Q&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?
“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.

That figure surpasses the 2025 Bybit theft, previously regarded as the largest known cryptocurrency heist on record. Binance's preliminary investigation identified a potentially compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, though the company later noted additional points of breach. Binance's preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as a likely entry point. Attackers may have used that access to reach a service container, then submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions from there. Binance said it found no evidence that private keys were leaked. Private keys are the cryptographic credentials that directly authorize control over cryptocurrency holdings, so their absence suggests attackers exploited an operational pathway rather than the most direct form of account control. The alleged method raises questions about whether privileged employee devices and associated environments had excessive access to systems capable of authorizing withdrawals at this scale. TRM Labs, Elliptic, and Chainalysis each attributed the attack to North Korea, though those assessments rest on blockchain tracing and pattern analysis rather than a completed criminal indictment. TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , describing it as an elite North Korean hacking unit. The firm said it reached that assessment with high confidence, according to Reuters. Elliptic cited similarities between this fund movement and patterns seen in earlier attacks linked to the same network, according to the Wall Street Journal. Chainalysis also assessed the breach as likely conducted by TraderTraitor, according to CBS News. Those assessments rest on blockchain tracing, infrastructure analysis, and attack-pattern comparison. No public criminal indictment has been filed in connection with this specific incident, and North Korean responsibility should be read as a converging set of private-sector assessments rather than a settled legal finding. User funds are safe, Binance asserted, though that claim remains unverified pending a full technical post-mortem and updated proof of reserves. User funds are safe, the company stated, and any losses will be covered through its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company reserves. Deployment access and financial authorization are different functions, and the incident raises questions about whether controls separating those functions were sufficient. Binance has not yet published a full technical post-mortem. Until it does, the complete picture of how this happened remains incomplete.

sources.title: Suspected North Korean hackers steal $5.6 billion in crypto in record-breaking cryptocurrency heist, Binance withdrawals frozen — firm says it will cover losses as stablecoin networks move to freeze $2.4b in stolen assets - Tom's Hardware
passages: From hereon, this month shall be called SpookITober.

In yet another high-profile cybersecurity incident this month, Binance.com, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hacked , to the tune of $5.6 billion taken in various cryptocurrencies.

As of this writing, withdrawals at the exchange are suspended until the company sorts out the situation, though it has stated repeatedly that "user funds remain safe," adding that it "will cover all losses." The U.S.-specific Binance.us website is so far reportedly unaffected.
At least two security agencies, including TRM , have pinned the attack on an elite North Korean hacking unit.
For what it's worth, the company has a means of insurance and a reasonable track record in these situations, though the amount of bullion pilfered today is exorbitant.
"TRM attributes this attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s premier hacking unit," the security firm said.
Per TRM, this latest instance bears many of the same hallmarks as earlier North Korean heists.

According to CNN , an unnamed analyst at Pangolin Intelligence corroborated this story by "Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]."
Back in May 2019, thieves made out with 7,000 BTC from Binance, amounting to around $40 million at the time.
The company covered the entirety of the losses with SAFU funds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

Preliminary info breaks down the stolen amounts like so: $1.57b in Tether dollars (USDT), $1.45b in Bitcoin (BTC), $875m in Ethereum (ETH), $823m in Circle dollars (USDC), $234m in Tron (TRX), $88.5m in Ripple dollars (RLUSD), $75M in Wrapped-Beacon Ethereum (WBETH), $50m in Tether Gold (XAUT), and $447.5 million in other cryptocurrencies.
Note that this is a developing story, so the tallies are subject to change.
Should that amount be final, this heist would exceed the $1.5b stolen from Bybit in February 2025, of which only a paltry portion has so far been recovered.
There's little info so far on the miscreant's means of larceny.

sources.body: From hereon, this month shall be called SpookITober. In yet another high-profile cybersecurity incident this month, Binance.com, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hacked , to the tune of $5.6 billion taken in various cryptocurrencies. As of this writing, withdrawals at the exchange are suspended until the company sorts out the situation, though it has stated repeatedly that "user funds remain safe," adding that it "will cover all losses." The U.S.-specific Binance.us website is so far reportedly unaffected. At least two security agencies, including TRM , have pinned the attack on an elite North Korean hacking unit. For what it's worth, the company has a means of insurance and a reasonable track record in these situations, though the amount of bullion pilfered today is exorbitant. "TRM attributes this attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s premier hacking unit," the security firm said. Per TRM, this latest instance bears many of the same hallmarks as earlier North Korean heists. According to CNN , an unnamed analyst at Pangolin Intelligence corroborated this story by "Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]." Back in May 2019, thieves made out with 7,000 BTC from Binance, amounting to around $40 million at the time. The company covered the entirety of the losses with SAFU funds. Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. Preliminary info breaks down the stolen amounts like so: $1.57b in Tether dollars (USDT), $1.45b in Bitcoin (BTC), $875m in Ethereum (ETH), $823m in Circle dollars (USDC), $234m in Tron (TRX), $88.5m in Ripple dollars (RLUSD), $75M in Wrapped-Beacon Ethereum (WBETH), $50m in Tether Gold (XAUT), and $447.5 million in other cryptocurrencies. Note that this is a developing story, so the tallies are subject to change. Should that amount be final, this heist would exceed the $1.5b stolen from Bybit in February 2025, of which only a paltry portion has so far been recovered. There's little info so far on the miscreant's means of larceny. Apparently, the Binance 14 , Binance 16 , and Hot Wallet 34 hot wallets, which hold pooled customer funds, were drained. It's currently not known if this happened via stolen private keys, a compromised signing process, or another type of intrusion. Update, Friday 30 Oct, 6:30 am ET: This developing story has been updated with information from Binance regarding how its system was compromised, and reports from security outlets claiming North Korea may be responsible. These details have been added to the story below. From hereon, this month shall be called SpookITober. In yet another high-profile cybersecurity incident this month, Binance.com, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hacked , to the tune of $5.6 billion taken in various cryptocurrencies. As of this writing, withdrawals at the exchange are suspended until the company sorts out the situation, though it has stated repeatedly that "user funds remain safe," adding that it "will cover all losses." The U.S.-specific Binance.us website is so far reportedly unaffected. At least two security agencies, including TRM , have pinned the attack on an elite North Korean hacking unit. "Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," the company said in an update on Friday. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it. We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." "TRM attributes this attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s premier hacking unit," the security firm said. "We base this assessment on robust on and off-chain intelligence sources," continuing to note that the group has been named responsible for a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. Per TRM, this latest instance bears many of the same hallmarks as earlier North Korean heists. According to CNN , an unnamed analyst at Pangolin Intelligence corroborated this story by "Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]." Preliminary info breaks down the stolen amounts like so: $1.57b in Tether dollars (USDT), $1.45b in Bitcoin (BTC), $875m in Ethereum (ETH), $823m in Circle dollars (USDC), $234m in Tron (TRX), $88.5m in Ripple dollars (RLUSD), $75M in Wrapped-Beacon Ethereum (WBETH), $50m in Tether Gold (XAUT), and $447.5 million in other cryptocurrencies. The "dollar" currencies are all stablecoins, meaning they're pegged to $1 to represent dollars in the virtual space. Meanwhile, Tether Gold is pegged to the value of one troy ounce. The stablecoin issuers all moved to blacklist the thief's main wallet (you can see it here on the Ethereum blockchain) in their smart contracts, a move that means the amounts in USDT, USDC, and RLUSD are frozen in place, totaling around $2.4 billion. It's possible, but not guaranteed, that the gold-pegged XAUT will also be frozen. Note that this does not mean those funds have been recovered — the thief simply cannot do anything with those tokens, be it moving or exchanging. Normally in these situations, restitution from the frozen funds happens only after complainants provide proof of ownership, something that usually means copious time spent in courts. The situation is a lot more grim for the amounts in pure cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, among others. From hereon, this month shall be called SpookITober. In yet another high-profile cybersecurity incident this month, Binance.com, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hacked , to the tune of $5.6 billion taken in various cryptocurrencies. As of this writing, withdrawals at the exchange are suspended until the company sorts out the situation, though it has stated repeatedly that "user funds remain safe," adding that it "will cover all losses." The U.S.-specific Binance.us website is so far reportedly unaffected. At least two security agencies, including TRM , have pinned the attack on an elite North Korean hacking unit.

"Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," the company said in an update on Friday. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it. We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."

"TRM attributes this attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s premier hacking unit," the security firm said. "We base this assessment on robust on and off-chain intelligence sources," continuing to note that the group has been named responsible for a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. Per TRM, this latest instance bears many of the same hallmarks as earlier North Korean heists. According to CNN , an unnamed analyst at Pangolin Intelligence corroborated this story by "Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]."

Preliminary info breaks down the stolen amounts like so: $1.57b in Tether dollars (USDT), $1.45b in Bitcoin (BTC), $875m in Ethereum (ETH), $823m in Circle dollars (USDC), $234m in Tron (TRX), $88.5m in Ripple dollars (RLUSD), $75M in Wrapped-Beacon Ethereum (WBETH), $50m in Tether Gold (XAUT), and $447.5 million in other cryptocurrencies. The "dollar" currencies are all stablecoins, meaning they're pegged to $1 to represent dollars in the virtual space. Meanwhile, Tether Gold is pegged to the value of one troy ounce.

The stablecoin issuers all moved to blacklist the thief's main wallet (you can see it here on the Ethereum blockchain) in their smart contracts, a move that means the amounts in USDT, USDC, and RLUSD are frozen in place, totaling around $2.4 billion. It's possible, but not guaranteed, that the gold-pegged XAUT will also be frozen.

Note that this does not mean those funds have been recovered — the thief simply cannot do anything with those tokens, be it moving or exchanging. Normally in these situations, restitution from the frozen funds happens only after complainants provide proof of ownership, something that usually means copious time spent in courts.

The situation is a lot more grim for the amounts in pure cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, among others. Since there is no governing entity for their blockchains, the most likely prospect is that the remaining $3.2 billion or so is forever lost in the ether — though some networks incorporate clawback mechanisms. Exchanges may block the thief when he eventually tries to cash out his virtual dough, but historically this hasn't been a reliable means of recovery.

That fund currently sits at 15,000 BTC in it (verifiable here ), or about $1.17b at the current BTC-USD price of $77,858. SAFU is a cold wallet, meaning its private keys are stored offline.
Back in May 2019, thieves made out with 7,000 BTC from Binance, amounting to around $40 million at the time. The company covered the entirety of the losses with SAFU funds.

sources.title: Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history - BBC
passages: Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.

Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".

The company said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach". Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack. Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record". AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody. The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens. The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past. Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets. Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement. In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them." In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets. "Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said. Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds. Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply. The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind. Cyber correspondent Joe Tidy explains more about what is suspected to be the biggest hack in history. sources.title: Binance Suspends Withdrawals After $6.3 Billion Cryptocurrency Hack as Bitcoin and Crypto Stocks Fall - Yahoo Finance
passages: Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals after reporting a security breach involving approximately $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, triggering losses across cryptocurrency markets and shares of companies exposed to the sector.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Bitcoin fell sharply following the announcement, while Ether, Binance's BNB token and several cryptocurrency-related stocks also recorded significant declines.
The attacker also withdrew 17,985 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $1.45 billion at the time.
Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market capitalisation, fell 2.5% to $78,106.60.
Binance said it had coordinated with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion of the assets affected by the attack.
The absence of a reported reduction in BNB holdings contrasted with the substantial losses involving Bitcoin, stablecoins and other cryptocurrencies.
The immediate focus for cryptocurrency markets will be Binance's progress in completing its security checks and restoring withdrawal services.
Binance indicated that it expects the suspension to last no longer than 48 hours, although the resumption of withdrawals remains dependent on the completion of its security procedures.
"It does look like a hack on Binance," Zhao said in a social media post.
Binance said its investigation had found no evidence that private keys associated with cryptocurrency wallets had been exposed.

Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals after reporting a security breach involving approximately $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, triggering losses across cryptocurrency markets and shares of companies exposed to the sector. The incident, disclosed on Thursday evening, represents the largest reported cryptocurrency theft on record, according to the exchange. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in affected assets and would cover all losses using its own funds. The exchange expects withdrawals to resume within 48 hours, subject to the completion of additional security checks. Bitcoin fell sharply following the announcement, while Ether, Binance's BNB token and several cryptocurrency-related stocks also recorded significant declines. Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, confirmed that an attacker had exploited a security vulnerability to carry out unauthorised withdrawals. The company estimated the total financial impact at $6.3 billion, making the incident substantially larger than previous cryptocurrency exchange hacks. According to Binance, the breach originated from a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The attacker used the compromised device to execute unauthorised withdrawals from the exchange. Binance said its investigation had found no evidence that private keys associated with cryptocurrency wallets had been exposed. The distinction is significant because private keys provide direct control over digital assets held in cryptocurrency wallets. The company has temporarily halted withdrawals while it conducts security checks and works to prevent further unauthorised transactions. Binance indicated that it expects the suspension to last no longer than 48 hours, although the resumption of withdrawals remains dependent on the completion of its security procedures. Binance said it had coordinated with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion of the assets affected by the attack. The exchange also committed to reimbursing all losses from its own financial resources. Circle, the company behind the USDC stablecoin, confirmed that it had frozen more than 800 million USDC linked to the breach. Tether separately reported freezing more than 1.567 billion USDT associated with the attack. The measures were intended to prevent the movement of stolen funds and limit the financial consequences of the incident. Binance co-founder and former Chief Executive Changpeng Zhao also commented on the situation. "It does look like a hack on Binance," Zhao said in a social media post. The company's commitment to cover losses and restore withdrawals will remain an important factor in determining how quickly confidence returns among its users. According to its data, the stolen assets included approximately $1.66 billion in Tether's USDT stablecoin. The attacker also withdrew 17,985 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $1.45 billion at the time. A further $767 million in USDC was transferred from the exchange. The figures illustrate the scale and diversity of the digital assets involved in the incident. Glassnode also reported that Binance's holdings of its native BNB token were "left untouched." The absence of a reported reduction in BNB holdings contrasted with the substantial losses involving Bitcoin, stablecoins and other cryptocurrencies. Cryptocurrency prices declined following the disclosure of the security breach, extending losses recorded earlier in the week. Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market capitalisation, fell 2.5% to $78,106.60. During the initial market reaction, the token dropped as low as $76,518 before recovering part of its losses. The selloff reflected concerns about exchange security, the potential impact on market liquidity and uncertainty surrounding the recovery of stolen assets. The temporary suspension of withdrawals also added to investor caution as Binance worked to complete its security review. The market reaction extended beyond cryptocurrencies to publicly traded companies with significant exposure to digital assets. The latest security incident introduced additional uncertainty for businesses whose performance is closely linked to the adoption and trading of digital assets. The immediate focus for cryptocurrency markets will be Binance's progress in completing its security checks and restoring withdrawal services. The exchange has indicated that withdrawals should resume within 48 hours and that it intends to absorb the financial losses associated with the incident.

sources.title: Binance pauses withdrawals as hackers suspected of stealing billions in crypto
passages: Crypto watchers say at least $2 billion has been drained from Binance’s hot wallets, which are internet-connected cryptocurrency wallets that store crypto that are connected to the internet.
By some estimates, Binance may have lost upward of $5.7 billion in crypto , though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing.
Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary said that Binance has “temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks following a security incident as a precautionary measure.”
“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement.

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”
Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered” but did not provide an explanation for the claim.
If confirmed into the billions, this would likely rank as one of the largest crypto breaches in history, according to leaderboards tracking crypto thefts.

coreStoryFacts.text: From hereon, this month shall be called SpookITober.

In yet another high-profile cybersecurity incident this month, Binance.com, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hacked , to the tune of $5.6 billion taken in various cryptocurrencies.

As of this writing, withdrawals at the exchange are suspended until the company sorts out the situation, though it has stated repeatedly that "user funds remain safe," adding that it "will cover all losses." The U.S.-specific Binance.us website is so far reportedly unaffected.
At least two security agencies, including TRM , have pinned the attack on an elite North Korean hacking unit.
For what it's worth, the company has a means of insurance and a reasonable track record in these situations, though the amount of bullion pilfered today is exorbitant.
"TRM attributes this attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s premier hacking unit," the security firm said.
Per TRM, this latest instance bears many of the same hallmarks as earlier North Korean heists.

According to CNN , an unnamed analyst at Pangolin Intelligence corroborated this story by "Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]."
Back in May 2019, thieves made out with 7,000 BTC from Binance, amounting to around $40 million at the time.
The company covered the entirety of the losses with SAFU funds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

Preliminary info breaks down the stolen amounts like so: $1.57b in Tether dollars (USDT), $1.45b in Bitcoin (BTC), $875m in Ethereum (ETH), $823m in Circle dollars (USDC), $234m in Tron (TRX), $88.5m in Ripple dollars (RLUSD), $75M in Wrapped-Beacon Ethereum (WBETH), $50m in Tether Gold (XAUT), and $447.5 million in other cryptocurrencies.
Note that this is a developing story, so the tallies are subject to change.
Should that amount be final, this heist would exceed the $1.5b stolen from Bybit in February 2025, of which only a paltry portion has so far been recovered.
There's little info so far on the miscreant's means of larceny.
Apparently, the Binance 14 , Binance 16 , and Hot Wallet 34 hot wallets, which hold pooled customer funds, were drained.
It's currently not known if this happened via stolen private keys, a compromised signing process, or another type of intrusion.

supportedClaims.text: From hereon, this month shall be called SpookITober.

In yet another high-profile cybersecurity incident this month, Binance.com, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hacked , to the tune of $5.6 billion taken in various cryptocurrencies.

As of this writing, withdrawals at the exchange are suspended until the company sorts out the situation, though it has stated repeatedly that "user funds remain safe," adding that it "will cover all losses." The U.S.-specific Binance.us website is so far reportedly unaffected.
At least two security agencies, including TRM , have pinned the attack on an elite North Korean hacking unit.
For what it's worth, the company has a means of insurance and a reasonable track record in these situations, though the amount of bullion pilfered today is exorbitant.
"TRM attributes this attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s premier hacking unit," the security firm said.
Per TRM, this latest instance bears many of the same hallmarks as earlier North Korean heists.

According to CNN , an unnamed analyst at Pangolin Intelligence corroborated this story by "Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]."
Back in May 2019, thieves made out with 7,000 BTC from Binance, amounting to around $40 million at the time.
The company covered the entirety of the losses with SAFU funds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

Preliminary info breaks down the stolen amounts like so: $1.57b in Tether dollars (USDT), $1.45b in Bitcoin (BTC), $875m in Ethereum (ETH), $823m in Circle dollars (USDC), $234m in Tron (TRX), $88.5m in Ripple dollars (RLUSD), $75M in Wrapped-Beacon Ethereum (WBETH), $50m in Tether Gold (XAUT), and $447.5 million in other cryptocurrencies.
Note that this is a developing story, so the tallies are subject to change.
Should that amount be final, this heist would exceed the $1.5b stolen from Bybit in February 2025, of which only a paltry portion has so far been recovered.
There's little info so far on the miscreant's means of larceny.
Apparently, the Binance 14 , Binance 16 , and Hot Wallet 34 hot wallets, which hold pooled customer funds, were drained.
It's currently not known if this happened via stolen private keys, a compromised signing process, or another type of intrusion.

The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.

Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".

Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals after reporting a security breach involving approximately $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, triggering losses across cryptocurrency markets and shares of companies exposed to the sector.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Bitcoin fell sharply following the announcement, while Ether, Binance's BNB token and several cryptocurrency-related stocks also recorded significant declines.
The attacker also withdrew 17,985 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $1.45 billion at the time.
Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market capitalisation, fell 2.5% to $78,106.60.
Binance said it had coordinated with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion of the assets affected by the attack.
The absence of a reported reduction in BNB holdings contrasted with the substantial losses involving Bitcoin, stablecoins and other cryptocurrencies.
The immediate focus for cryptocurrency markets will be Binance's progress in completing its security checks and restoring withdrawal services.
Binance indicated that it expects the suspension to last no longer than 48 hours, although the resumption of withdrawals remains dependent on the completion of its security procedures.
"It does look like a hack on Binance," Zhao said in a social media post.
Binance said its investigation had found no evidence that private keys associated with cryptocurrency wallets had been exposed.
Crypto watchers say at least $2 billion has been drained from Binance’s hot wallets, which are internet-connected cryptocurrency wallets that store crypto that are connected to the internet.
By some estimates, Binance may have lost upward of $5.7 billion in crypto , though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing.
Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary said that Binance has “temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks following a security incident as a precautionary measure.”
“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement.

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”
Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered” but did not provide an explanation for the claim.
If confirmed into the billions, this would likely rank as one of the largest crypto breaches in history, according to leaderboards tracking crypto thefts.

sources.title: Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history - BBC
passages: Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.

Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".

The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses". The company said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach". Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack. Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record". AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody. The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens. The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past. Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets. Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement. In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them." In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets. "Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said. Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds. Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply. The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind. Cyber correspondent Joe Tidy explains more about what is suspected to be the biggest hack in history. passages: Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals after reporting a security breach involving approximately $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, triggering losses across cryptocurrency markets and shares of companies exposed to the sector.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Bitcoin fell sharply following the announcement, while Ether, Binance's BNB token and several cryptocurrency-related stocks also recorded significant declines.
The attacker also withdrew 17,985 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $1.45 billion at the time.
Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market capitalisation, fell 2.5% to $78,106.60.
Binance said it had coordinated with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion of the assets affected by the attack.
The absence of a reported reduction in BNB holdings contrasted with the substantial losses involving Bitcoin, stablecoins and other cryptocurrencies.
The immediate focus for cryptocurrency markets will be Binance's progress in completing its security checks and restoring withdrawal services.
Binance indicated that it expects the suspension to last no longer than 48 hours, although the resumption of withdrawals remains dependent on the completion of its security procedures.
"It does look like a hack on Binance," Zhao said in a social media post.
Binance said its investigation had found no evidence that private keys associated with cryptocurrency wallets had been exposed.

By some estimates, Binance may have lost upward of $5.7 billion in crypto , though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing.
Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary said that Binance has “temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks following a security incident as a precautionary measure.”
“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement.

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”
Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered” but did not provide an explanation for the claim.
If confirmed into the billions, this would likely rank as one of the largest crypto breaches in history, according to leaderboards tracking crypto thefts.

sources.title: OpenAI CEO says it's 'quite terrible' for your PC to have RAM — Sam Altman says data centers offer better utilization - Tom's Hardware
passages: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem.
In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home.

Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down.
It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.
Freedman is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware focusing on laptops, desktops and gaming.
A lover of all things gaming and tech, his previous work has shown up in Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, Kotaku, PCMag and Complex, among others.
Follow him on Threads @FreedmanAE and BlueSky @andrewfreedman.net .
You can send him tips on Signal: andrewfreedman.01

He said local AI inference, which is becoming an increasingly popular alternative to cloud-based AI services, leaves memory unused most of the time, making it a poor allocation of scarce DRAM. Altman's position also aligns with OpenAI's business model. Although the company offers some open-weight models, its main products are closed-source models that run in data centers and are accessed through subscriptions and cloud services. Wider adoption of local AI models could reduce users’ dependence on cloud platforms and subscriptions, although data centers would remain essential for training large models. coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem.
In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home.

Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down.
It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.
