Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers.

Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years.
From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment, - Sam Altman .
Remarks come as AI infrastructure providers compete for increasingly limited memory supplies.
Memory manufacturers are prioritizing demand from data centers, putting additional pressure on the consumer market and contributing to higher prices for PCs and other hardware.
In other words, Altman believes memory would be put to better use in centralized data centers, where it could continuously serve multiple users and workloads.
However, his argument focuses on local AI inference and does not account for the many other reasons people need RAM in their PCs, including gaming, everyday applications and multitasking.
Altman’s claim that idle consumer RAM wastes a global resource draws scrutiny given OpenAI’s direct financial stake in cloud computing

From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment, - Sam Altman .
Remarks come as AI infrastructure providers compete for increasingly limited memory supplies.
Memory manufacturers are prioritizing demand from data centers, putting additional pressure on the consumer market and contributing to higher prices for PCs and other hardware.
In other words, Altman believes memory would be put to better use in centralized data centers, where it could continuously serve multiple users and workloads.
However, his argument focuses on local AI inference and does not account for the many other reasons people need RAM in their PCs, including gaming, everyday applications and multitasking.

story.title: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk

facts.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem.
In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home.

Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.
Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down.
It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally.
The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.
Freedman is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware focusing on laptops, desktops and gaming.
A lover of all things gaming and tech, his previous work has shown up in Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, Kotaku, PCMag and Complex, among others.

sources.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem. In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible." OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud. Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down. It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally. The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics. With data centers full of RAM, your PC is apparently the problem.
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has data centers full of memory, but seemingly it's the 32GB of RAM in your desktop that's the problem. In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build. Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark):

"From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."
While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model.

OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud. Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down. It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally. The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.

extraction.body: When you buy through our links, you’re supporting our mission . Altman’s claim that idle consumer RAM wastes a global resource draws scrutiny given OpenAI’s direct financial stake in cloud computing Altman reportedly argued on the Cheeky Pint podcast that local AI inference creates a poor allocation of scarce DRAM . Local inference means running AI models directly on personal devices rather than through cloud servers. DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory, is the short-term working memory inside computers, phones, and servers. According to that reported account, Altman called it quite terrible from a global-allocation standpoint for individuals to hold memory sitting unused roughly 95% of the time. He argued that pooled data-center memory could theoretically run at far higher utilization rates than consumer devices allow. He also reportedly referenced an OpenAI-designed AI processor called “Jalapeno” and argued that the world shares an interest in using limited silicon efficiently. No primary source confirming the chip’s specifications or production status was available at the time of writing. Both the chip details and the podcast characterizations should be treated as reported rather than verified until a transcript or recording is confirmed. A major memory manufacturer is leaving the consumer market, and AI demand is the stated reason. Micron announced in December 2025 that it would exit its Crucial consumer memory business. The company cited surging AI-driven demand, and said redirecting resources would allow it to support larger strategic customers in faster-growing segments, according to its investor press release. HBM , or high-bandwidth memory, is a specialized chip built for AI accelerators. Reuters reported simultaneous pressure across DRAM, NAND flash, and HBM markets, affecting products from PCs to smartphones. Micron’s decision reflects a manufacturer prioritizing enterprise and AI customers over consumers. It does not establish that consumer devices are the primary cause of the supply crunch. Capacity allocation, investment decisions, and corporate pricing strategy are also significant factors. Altman’s utilization logic points toward centralized cloud services, which OpenAI sells. OpenAI operates large-scale AI infrastructure and generates revenue when users access its models through cloud subscriptions. Users running open-source models locally on their own hardware represent a competing path that does not flow through OpenAI’s systems. Altman’s utilization argument, whatever its technical merits, aligns with his company’s commercial interests. That does not make the argument wrong, but it is a relevant consideration alongside the engineering rationale. A car parked in a garage is not a failed resource allocation. Running models locally can improve privacy, preserve offline availability, and give users resilience when centralized services go down. Personal hardware that sits idle most of the day still delivers value by being ready when needed, much like a home appliance. Concentrating memory in centralized data centers also concentrates decision-making power among a small number of companies. Users can become dependent on subscription terms and remote access policies they did not set and cannot change. These are ownership and policy questions, not purely engineering ones. Utilization efficiency is one principle. It is not the only one. Memory shortages are real, and manufacturer priorities are shifting toward AI infrastructure. Whether those pressures should also determine who owns and controls personal computing hardware is a separate question. Accepting utilization as the governing principle for hardware ownership would shift significant computing power away from individuals and toward a small number of AI data centers . That shift is worth examining before it becomes the assumed default. Concentrating memory in centralized data centers also concentrates decision-making power among a small number of companies. Users can become dependent on subscription terms and remote access policies they did not set and cannot change. These are ownership and policy questions, not purely engineering ones.
Utilization efficiency is one principle. It is not the only one.

Memory shortages are real, and manufacturer priorities are shifting toward AI infrastructure. Whether those pressures should also determine who owns and controls personal computing hardware is a separate question.

Accepting utilization as the governing principle for hardware ownership would shift significant computing power away from individuals and toward a small number of AI data centers . That shift is worth examining before it becomes the assumed default.

Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post Friday morning that customer withdrawals should resume within 48 hours. "We are rebuilding the withdrawal service, and we are not switching it back until it passes rigorous testing," noted Teng on Friday. "We are very hopeful that users will be able to withdraw prior to the Sunday deadline." Teng said the hack was not carried out by one person. Initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but further review revealed broader security breaches. "This was a complex attack," Teng said. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers." The attack has rattled crypto markets and related stocks. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) tumbled 5% to hover below $77,000 on Friday. Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping 4% to around $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also plunged by more than 6%. Crypto-related stocks traded lower, led by shares of Circle, trading platforms Coinbase ( COIN ) and Robinhood ( HOOD ), and digital-asset Treasury giant Strategy ( MSTR ). Binance said that about $3 billion in assets have been "frozen on-chain so far." The frozen assets include over $2 billion in stablecoins. Tether, the world's largest stablecoin issuer, "froze more than 1.567B" of its USDT stablecoin in relation to the hack," CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X . The second-largest issuer, Circle ( CRCL ), froze another $800 million "in coordination with law enforcement," CEO Jeremy Allaire said. World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency venture co-founded by President Trump and his sons, said it froze $27 million of its stablecoin, USD1, associated with the hack, according to CEO Zack Witkoff. Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack. "That meaningfully reduces the risk of a negative feedback loop involving withdrawals, forced selling, tighter credit, and broader deleveraging," he added. An “initial investigation” suggested hackers had been able to compromise an engineer’s laptop and withdraw funds from the platform, Binance said, adding on Friday morning that further investigation “has uncovered additional points of breach.” The company is working with law enforcement. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs linked the hack with a North Korean unit known as TraderTraitor, saying that the sums involved would make it “the largest crypto theft on record.” Last year, North Korean hackers stole crypto worth $1.5 billion in an attack on exchange Bybit. Peter Ward, of the Sejong Institute in Seoul, said North Korea had considerable expertise and offered “near-total protection to its hackers.” “Things may get a lot worse going forward,” he said. Binance said on Friday that it had “already reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident,” with $5 billion of the funds “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.” The company said it was actively buying more tokens in order to cover the remaining amount. “This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity,” and settlement “also takes time,” it said. The hack is a major blow to Binance, which was co-founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao and holds about $140 billion of digital assets. In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to US criminal charges related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine. Zhao, known as CZ, pleaded guilty to criminal charges relating to inadequate money laundering controls. He stepped down as chief executive and was pardoned last year by US President Donald Trump. The crypto market is in the grip of a prolonged downturn after a sharp sell-off late last year wiped more than $1tn from the combined capitalization of about 18,000 digital tokens. Richard Teng, co-chief executive of Binance, told customers that their “money is safe, and we’re covering every loss” from a reserve fund as well as “company funds.” Binance’s reserve fund holds about $1 billion worth of bitcoin, according to a company update from mid-October. Zhao said this leaves roughly $2 billion that the company still needs to cover, adding that the company owns shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX worth more than $1 billion. “Remaining gap is (still painful, but) manageable,” he said in a post on X. Binance co-chief executive Yi He said on Friday that the company’s annual revenue “is sufficient to cover the losses,” without giving further details. CZ said earlier this year that the company’s annual revenue is about $5 billion. Crypto venues have become lucrative targets for hackers, with notable heists including $280 million stolen in April from the coffers of unregulated crypto exchange Drift. Unlike traditional exchanges, crypto venues sit on big piles of customer assets. Some institutional investors in recent years have sought third-party custody arrangements in order to keep their funds elsewhere and mitigate the risks of their assets being stolen directly off the exchange. The exchange, which became regulated in Abu Dhabi in December 2025, had already agreed to block UK customers from signing up for the exchange after being barred by Britain’s financial watchdog in 2021. In the US, Binance operates under a separate entity from the rest of its global operations that is registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and authorized to operate as a money transmitter in 32 states. North Korean hackers stole about $2 billion in cryptocurrency in 2025, a 50 percent increase from the year before, according to data from Chainalysis. Binance said it found no evidence that unique user codes, known as “private keys,” had been breached. In a post on X early on Friday, Yi He said the exchange expected to allow withdrawals again “in the next 48 hours.” Binance, which has no official headquarters, last year became regulated in Abu Dhabi, where Zhao and He, who are romantic partners, are based. Jeremy Allaire, head of Circle, the second-biggest stablecoin issuer, said $800 million of its USDC coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit” at Binance. Crypto companies can freeze the wallets in which stolen funds are moved or held. extraction.body: SINGAPORE/PARIS/BOSTON: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. Cryptocurrency prices fell ​on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets. The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion. Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion. “We NEVER use any customer funds, so they are not impacted,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said ‌in a post on ‌X. Teng described the breach as a “complex attack” that was not carried out by one person and ​included ‌a ⁠compromised laptop ​as well ⁠as malicious software designed to delete traces and evidence of its activity as it went along, “making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate.” The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, Internet-connected wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said. Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs ⁠and Chainalysis. TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a ‌2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea. “TRM attributes the attack ‌to ... North Korea’s elite hacking unit,” the firm said in an analysis on its website. Both TRM ​and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible. “This incident ‌is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for ‌espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts. North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters. The FBI said it was “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate ‌investigative steps.” The USSS did not respond to an emailed request for comment. Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating license, said it was “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident.” “It’s the biggest ⁠hack in history,” Aravind Srinivasan at market ⁠maker GSR said, as crypto prices fell broadly. Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3 percent to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilized.

coreStoryFacts.text: North Korean hackers swiped $2 billion in 2025 , bringing the rogue regime's total haul since 2016 through the end of last year to $6.75 billion, according to data from crypto firm Chainalysis.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, was hit late Thursday by what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history , with $6.3 billion in funds impacted and roughly half of those assets frozen.

"This is likely the largest crypto hack on record, but the key distinction is that it does not currently appear to be a solvency event for Binance," Fundstrat head of digital assets Sean Farrell said.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping 4% to around $2,200.
Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also plunged by more than 6%.

The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms.
Binance, in its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests the incident may have begun with a compromised engineer's laptop.
The exchange added that it has found no evidence that wallet passwords were leaked.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter at Yahoo Finance.
Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post Friday morning that customer withdrawals should resume within 48 hours.
Binance said it has money set aside in a Secure Asset Fund for Users to handle extreme cases, such as security breaches.

The exchange put the “estimated total impact” of the hack at about $6.3 billion and said around $3 billion of affected assets, mainly stablecoins that act as cash for the crypto market, had been frozen.
In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to US criminal charges related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine.

Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs linked the hack with a North Korean unit known as TraderTraitor, saying that the sums involved would make it “the largest crypto theft on record.” Last year, North Korean hackers stole crypto worth $1.5 billion in an attack on exchange Bybit.
Binance scrambles to freeze billions after record-breaking hack linked to North Korea.

Richard Teng, co-chief executive of Binance, told customers that their “money is safe, and we’re covering every loss” from a reserve fund as well as “company funds.” Binance’s reserve fund holds about $1 billion worth of bitcoin, according to a company update from mid-October.

An “initial investigation” suggested hackers had been able to compromise an engineer’s laptop and withdraw funds from the platform, Binance said, adding on Friday morning that further investigation “has uncovered additional points of breach.” The company is working with law enforcement.
Binance has suspended all withdrawals after the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange fell victim to what appears to be the biggest heist in history.
Crypto venues have become lucrative targets for hackers, with notable heists including $280 million stolen in April from the coffers of unregulated crypto exchange Drift.

Analytics firm Elliptic said it had verified $2.8 billion of frozen crypto—mostly USDT and USDC—but that the hackers had moved the remainder into assets that could not be frozen, such as the ETH crypto token.
Binance was ordered to wind down its EU operations in July after it failed to secure a license under the bloc’s new regulatory framework.
Binance works with Swiss banks Sygnum and Flow, the FT previously reported.

In the US, Binance operates under a separate entity from the rest of its global operations that is registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and authorized to operate as a money transmitter in 32 states.

extraction.body: Binance scrambles to freeze billions after record-breaking hack linked to North Korea. Binance has suspended all withdrawals after the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange fell victim to what appears to be the biggest heist in history. The exchange put the “estimated total impact” of the hack at about $6.3 billion and said around $3 billion of affected assets, mainly stablecoins that act as cash for the crypto market, had been frozen. But analysts at Elliptic said the attacker had changed about $3.3 billion into digital assets that could not be frozen and was working to cash those out as traditional currency. An “initial investigation” suggested hackers had been able to compromise an engineer’s laptop and withdraw funds from the platform, Binance said, adding on Friday morning that further investigation “has uncovered additional points of breach.” The company is working with law enforcement. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs linked the hack with a North Korean unit known as TraderTraitor, saying that the sums involved would make it “the largest crypto theft on record.” Last year, North Korean hackers stole crypto worth $1.5 billion in an attack on exchange Bybit. Peter Ward, of the Sejong Institute in Seoul, said North Korea had considerable expertise and offered “near-total protection to its hackers.” “Things may get a lot worse going forward,” he said. Binance said on Friday that it had “already reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident,” with $5 billion of the funds “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.” The company said it was actively buying more tokens in order to cover the remaining amount. “This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity,” and settlement “also takes time,” it said. The hack is a major blow to Binance, which was co-founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao and holds about $140 billion of digital assets. In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to US criminal charges related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine. Zhao, known as CZ, pleaded guilty to criminal charges relating to inadequate money laundering controls. He stepped down as chief executive and was pardoned last year by US President Donald Trump. The crypto market is in the grip of a prolonged downturn after a sharp sell-off late last year wiped more than $1tn from the combined capitalization of about 18,000 digital tokens. Richard Teng, co-chief executive of Binance, told customers that their “money is safe, and we’re covering every loss” from a reserve fund as well as “company funds.” Binance’s reserve fund holds about $1 billion worth of bitcoin, according to a company update from mid-October. Zhao said this leaves roughly $2 billion that the company still needs to cover, adding that the company owns shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX worth more than $1 billion. “Remaining gap is (still painful, but) manageable,” he said in a post on X. Binance co-chief executive Yi He said on Friday that the company’s annual revenue “is sufficient to cover the losses,” without giving further details. CZ said earlier this year that the company’s annual revenue is about $5 billion. Crypto venues have become lucrative targets for hackers, with notable heists including $280 million stolen in April from the coffers of unregulated crypto exchange Drift. Unlike traditional exchanges, crypto venues sit on big piles of customer assets. Some institutional investors in recent years have sought third-party custody arrangements in order to keep their funds elsewhere and mitigate the risks of their assets being stolen directly off the exchange. Binance works with Swiss banks Sygnum and Flow, the FT previously reported. Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which regulates Binance’s main global crypto exchange, said in a statement on Friday that it was aware of the “security incident involving unauthorized withdrawals of assets” from the company’s exchange and was “engaging closely with Binance.” Binance was ordered to wind down its EU operations in July after it failed to secure a license under the bloc’s new regulatory framework. The exchange, which became regulated in Abu Dhabi in December 2025, had already agreed to block UK customers from signing up for the exchange after being barred by Britain’s financial watchdog in 2021. In the US, Binance operates under a separate entity from the rest of its global operations that is registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and authorized to operate as a money transmitter in 32 states. Last month, nearly $390 million was stolen from crypto exchange Bitget, which reimbursed customers from its so-called User Protection Fund. North Korean hackers stole about $2 billion in cryptocurrency in 2025, a 50 percent increase from the year before, according to data from Chainalysis. Binance said it found no evidence that unique user codes, known as “private keys,” had been breached. In a post on X early on Friday, Yi He said the exchange expected to allow withdrawals again “in the next 48 hours.” Binance, which has no official headquarters, last year became regulated in Abu Dhabi, where Zhao and He, who are romantic partners, are based. In a sign of the potential repercussions from the heist, Paolo Ardoino, chief executive of Tether, said his company had frozen about $1.5 billion of USDT, its $180 billion dollar-linked stablecoin. Jeremy Allaire, head of Circle, the second-biggest stablecoin issuer, said $800 million of its USDC coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit” at Binance. Crypto companies can freeze the wallets in which stolen funds are moved or held. Analytics firm Elliptic said it had verified $2.8 billion of frozen crypto—mostly USDT and USDC—but that the hackers had moved the remainder into assets that could not be frozen, such as the ETH crypto token. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” Elliptic said.

But analysts at Elliptic said the attacker had changed about $3.3 billion into digital assets that could not be frozen and was working to cash those out as traditional currency.

An “initial investigation” suggested hackers had been able to compromise an engineer’s laptop and withdraw funds from the platform, Binance said, adding on Friday morning that further investigation “has uncovered additional points of breach.” The company is working with law enforcement.

Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs linked the hack with a North Korean unit known as TraderTraitor, saying that the sums involved would make it “the largest crypto theft on record.” Last year, North Korean hackers stole crypto worth $1.5 billion in an attack on exchange Bybit.
Peter Ward, of the Sejong Institute in Seoul, said North Korea had considerable expertise and offered “near-total protection to its hackers.”
“Things may get a lot worse going forward,” he said.

Binance said on Friday that it had “already reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident,” with $5 billion of the funds “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.”

The company said it was actively buying more tokens in order to cover the remaining amount. “This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity,” and settlement “also takes time,” it said.

The hack is a major blow to Binance, which was co-founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao and holds about $140 billion of digital assets. In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to US criminal charges related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine.
Zhao, known as CZ, pleaded guilty to criminal charges relating to inadequate money laundering controls. He stepped down as chief executive and was pardoned last year by US President Donald Trump.
The crypto market is in the grip of a prolonged downturn after a sharp sell-off late last year wiped more than $1tn from the combined capitalization of about 18,000 digital tokens.

Richard Teng, co-chief executive of Binance, told customers that their “money is safe, and we’re covering every loss” from a reserve fund as well as “company funds.” Binance’s reserve fund holds about $1 billion worth of bitcoin, according to a company update from mid-October.
Zhao said this leaves roughly $2 billion that the company still needs to cover, adding that the company owns shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX worth more than $1 billion.
“Remaining gap is (still painful, but) manageable,” he said in a post on X.

Binance co-chief executive Yi He said on Friday that the company’s annual revenue “is sufficient to cover the losses,” without giving further details. CZ said earlier this year that the company’s annual revenue is about $5 billion.
Crypto venues have become lucrative targets for hackers, with notable heists including $280 million stolen in April from the coffers of unregulated crypto exchange Drift.

Unlike traditional exchanges, crypto venues sit on big piles of customer assets. Some institutional investors in recent years have sought third-party custody arrangements in order to keep their funds elsewhere and mitigate the risks of their assets being stolen directly off the exchange.
Binance works with Swiss banks Sygnum and Flow, the FT previously reported.

Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which regulates Binance’s main global crypto exchange, said in a statement on Friday that it was aware of the “security incident involving unauthorized withdrawals of assets” from the company’s exchange and was “engaging closely with Binance.”

Binance was ordered to wind down its EU operations in July after it failed to secure a license under the bloc’s new regulatory framework. The exchange, which became regulated in Abu Dhabi in December 2025, had already agreed to block UK customers from signing up for the exchange after being barred by Britain’s financial watchdog in 2021.

In the US, Binance operates under a separate entity from the rest of its global operations that is registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and authorized to operate as a money transmitter in 32 states.
Last month, nearly $390 million was stolen from crypto exchange Bitget, which reimbursed customers from its so-called User Protection Fund.
North Korean hackers stole about $2 billion in cryptocurrency in 2025, a 50 percent increase from the year before, according to data from Chainalysis.
Binance said it found no evidence that unique user codes, known as “private keys,” had been breached.
In a post on X early on Friday, Yi He said the exchange expected to allow withdrawals again “in the next 48 hours.”
Binance, which has no official headquarters, last year became regulated in Abu Dhabi, where Zhao and He, who are romantic partners, are based.
In a sign of the potential repercussions from the heist, Paolo Ardoino, chief executive of Tether, said his company had frozen about $1.5 billion of USDT, its $180 billion dollar-linked stablecoin.
Jeremy Allaire, head of Circle, the second-biggest stablecoin issuer, said $800 million of its USDC coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit” at Binance.

Crypto companies can freeze the wallets in which stolen funds are moved or held. Analytics firm Elliptic said it had verified $2.8 billion of frozen crypto—mostly USDT and USDC—but that the hackers had moved the remainder into assets that could not be frozen, such as the ETH crypto token.
“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” Elliptic said.

Both TRM ​and Chainalysis said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible. “This incident ‌is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for ‌espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts. North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters. The FBI said it was “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate ‌investigative steps.” The USSS did not respond to an emailed request for comment. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals after reporting a security breach involving approximately $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, triggering losses across cryptocurrency markets and shares of companies exposed to the sector. The incident, disclosed on Thursday evening, represents the largest reported cryptocurrency theft on record, according to the exchange. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in affected assets and would cover all losses using its own funds. The exchange expects withdrawals to resume within 48 hours, subject to the completion of additional security checks. Bitcoin fell sharply following the announcement, while Ether, Binance's BNB token and several cryptocurrency-related stocks also recorded significant declines. Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, confirmed that an attacker had exploited a security vulnerability to carry out unauthorised withdrawals. The company estimated the total financial impact at $6.3 billion, making the incident substantially larger than previous cryptocurrency exchange hacks. According to Binance, the breach originated from a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The attacker used the compromised device to execute unauthorised withdrawals from the exchange. Binance said its investigation had found no evidence that private keys associated with cryptocurrency wallets had been exposed. The distinction is significant because private keys provide direct control over digital assets held in cryptocurrency wallets. The company has temporarily halted withdrawals while it conducts security checks and works to prevent further unauthorised transactions. Binance indicated that it expects the suspension to last no longer than 48 hours, although the resumption of withdrawals remains dependent on the completion of its security procedures. Binance said it had coordinated with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion of the assets affected by the attack. The exchange also committed to reimbursing all losses from its own financial resources. Circle, the company behind the USDC stablecoin, confirmed that it had frozen more than 800 million USDC linked to the breach. Tether separately reported freezing more than 1.567 billion USDT associated with the attack. The measures were intended to prevent the movement of stolen funds and limit the financial consequences of the incident. Binance co-founder and former Chief Executive Changpeng Zhao also commented on the situation. "It does look like a hack on Binance," Zhao said in a social media post. The company's commitment to cover losses and restore withdrawals will remain an important factor in determining how quickly confidence returns among its users. According to its data, the stolen assets included approximately $1.66 billion in Tether's USDT stablecoin. The attacker also withdrew 17,985 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $1.45 billion at the time. A further $767 million in USDC was transferred from the exchange. The figures illustrate the scale and diversity of the digital assets involved in the incident. Glassnode also reported that Binance's holdings of its native BNB token were "left untouched." The absence of a reported reduction in BNB holdings contrasted with the substantial losses involving Bitcoin, stablecoins and other cryptocurrencies. Cryptocurrency prices declined following the disclosure of the security breach, extending losses recorded earlier in the week. Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market capitalisation, fell 2.5% to $78,106.60. During the initial market reaction, the token dropped as low as $76,518 before recovering part of its losses. The selloff reflected concerns about exchange security, the potential impact on market liquidity and uncertainty surrounding the recovery of stolen assets. The temporary suspension of withdrawals also added to investor caution as Binance worked to complete its security review. The market reaction extended beyond cryptocurrencies to publicly traded companies with significant exposure to digital assets. The latest security incident introduced additional uncertainty for businesses whose performance is closely linked to the adoption and trading of digital assets. The immediate focus for cryptocurrency markets will be Binance's progress in completing its security checks and restoring withdrawal services. The exchange has indicated that withdrawals should resume within 48 hours and that it intends to absorb the financial losses associated with the incident.

sources.title: It Took Hackers Just 20 Minutes to Steal $6.3 Billion in Crypto from a Single Platform - Futurism
passages: Crypto exchange Binance suspended withdrawals after elite hackers stole a staggering $6.3 billion in digital assets, marking what may be the biggest crypto heist of all time.

Researchers at the crypto research firm TRM Labs told the New York Times that they have “high confidence” in its assessment that the theft was the work of “North Korea’s elite hacking unit.” It reportedly took just 20 minutes to drain Binance of billions of dollars in crypto.
Previously, crypto’s biggest heist was last February’s attack on Binance rival Bybit, according to NYT .
That attack was also carried out by North Korean hackers, who made away with $1.5 billion.
Crypto has always been risky — and even riskier now that cybercriminals have access to advanced AI tools that are supercharging hacking efforts across the digital world.
I’m a senior staff writer at Futurism, investigating how the rise of artificial intelligence is impacting the media, internet, and information ecosystems.

Binance founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao said on X that “user funds are safe,” but the incident “does look like a hack.” Zhao, a major player in the crypto world, pleaded guilty to money laundering and was sentenced to four months in prison in 2024 but was pardoned last year by president Donald Trump after Binance provided support to World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s much-scrutinized crypto venture. (Zhao is no longer Binance’s CEO, but is still a shareholder.)

passages: North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.”

State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations.
A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI.
US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program.
Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news.
Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion.
Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m.
ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders.
Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets.
Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop.

In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person.
Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet.
“We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses.
It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack.

North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.” Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m. ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders. Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person. The culprits targeted just a few accounts, including one crypto wallet holding nearly $800 million, Idan Ofrat, co-founder of Fireblocks, told The Post. TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program. Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms. The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack. Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.” Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion. “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!” Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West. “You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, also called it the “largest bank heist in human history.” Binance said it is working with law enforcement, including the Secret Service; blockchain intelligence firms; token issuers; and other exchanges to trace and recover the stolen funds, promising to do everything possible to “ensure that these bad actors will be held accountable.” Crypto and law enforcement officials are now in a “cat and mouse game” against the North Korean hackers, racing to recover the stolen crypto before it’s turned into fiat currency and hidden forever, CNBC reported. Stablecoin providers – which tie digital assets to currencies like the dollar with a 1:1 ratio – could reissue the tokens, potentially recovering the losses. But the hackers have already sold the stablecoins and borrowed ether, which is more difficult to freeze, according to CNBC. The exchange is also conducting a full security review across the company, including endpoints, cloud and key management, according to Teng. The company said there is no evidence of the hacker still having direct access to funds. TRM Labs, the US-based blockchain intelligence firm that pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, described the cybercriminal group as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.” A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI. Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget. State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations. Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet. The exchange holds a total of $167 billion in crypto assets across its digital wallets, according to blockchain analytics firm Nansen.

coreStoryFacts.text: Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals after reporting a security breach involving approximately $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, triggering losses across cryptocurrency markets and shares of companies exposed to the sector.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Bitcoin fell sharply following the announcement, while Ether, Binance's BNB token and several cryptocurrency-related stocks also recorded significant declines.
The attacker also withdrew 17,985 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $1.45 billion at the time.
Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market capitalisation, fell 2.5% to $78,106.60.
Binance said it had coordinated with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion of the assets affected by the attack.
The absence of a reported reduction in BNB holdings contrasted with the substantial losses involving Bitcoin, stablecoins and other cryptocurrencies.
The immediate focus for cryptocurrency markets will be Binance's progress in completing its security checks and restoring withdrawal services.
Binance indicated that it expects the suspension to last no longer than 48 hours, although the resumption of withdrawals remains dependent on the completion of its security procedures.
"It does look like a hack on Binance," Zhao said in a social media post.
Binance said its investigation had found no evidence that private keys associated with cryptocurrency wallets had been exposed.
Binance has confirmed to TechCrunch that it is dealing with a security incident as users reported that funds were being drained from the crypto exchange’s wallets.
By some estimates, Binance may have lost upward of $5.7 billion in crypto , though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing.
Financial tech giant Circle froze about $800 million in Tether as it passed through its networks, while crypto giant Tether froze about $1.56 billion related to Binance’s hack.
“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement.

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”
Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered” but did not provide an explanation for the claim.

sources.title: It Took Hackers Just 20 Minutes to Steal $6.3 Billion in Crypto from a Single Platform - Futurism
passages: Crypto exchange Binance suspended withdrawals after elite hackers stole a staggering $6.3 billion in digital assets, marking what may be the biggest crypto heist of all time.

Researchers at the crypto research firm TRM Labs told the New York Times that they have “high confidence” in its assessment that the theft was the work of “North Korea’s elite hacking unit.” It reportedly took just 20 minutes to drain Binance of billions of dollars in crypto.
Previously, crypto’s biggest heist was last February’s attack on Binance rival Bybit, according to NYT .
That attack was also carried out by North Korean hackers, who made away with $1.5 billion.
Crypto has always been risky — and even riskier now that cybercriminals have access to advanced AI tools that are supercharging hacking efforts across the digital world.
I’m a senior staff writer at Futurism, investigating how the rise of artificial intelligence is impacting the media, internet, and information ecosystems.

Binance founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao said on X that “user funds are safe,” but the incident “does look like a hack.” Zhao, a major player in the crypto world, pleaded guilty to money laundering and was sentenced to four months in prison in 2024 but was pardoned last year by president Donald Trump after Binance provided support to World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s much-scrutinized crypto venture. (Zhao is no longer Binance’s CEO, but is still a shareholder.)

sources.title: North Korean hackers steal $6.3B from Binance in ‘largest bank heist in human history’ - New York Post
passages: North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.”

State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations.
A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI.
US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program.
Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news.
Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion.
Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m.
ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders.
Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets.
Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop.

In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person.
Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet.
“We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses.
It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack.

Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person. The culprits targeted just a few accounts, including one crypto wallet holding nearly $800 million, Idan Ofrat, co-founder of Fireblocks, told The Post. TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program. Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms. The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack. Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.” Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion. “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!” Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West. “You could probably say it was the biggest hack ever in terms of monetary value,” Nic Puckrin, CEO of Coin Bureau, told The Post. Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget. While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet. sources.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow - The Business Times
passages: The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI. Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines. sources.title: AI spending is soaring, but where is the revenue? Anand Shah flags cracks in the boom
passages: Anand Shah, CIO of PMS & AIF at ICICI Prudential AMC, sees cracks emerging in the artificial intelligence investment boom as revenue generation fails to keep pace with spending on infrastructure.
He believes the sustainability of the massive investment cycle will depend on how effectively AI companies convert spending into revenue.“Today, the boom is in AI investment.

We are not seeing a big boom in terms of revenue,” Shah told CNBC-TV18 in an interview.He pointed to pressure on companies supplying AI infrastructure, including chip manufacturers and businesses benefiting from electrification, alongside revenue concerns among AI companies.

He argued that the country would continue to need foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investor flows unless exports increased significantly relative to imports.Shah also noted that the securities transaction tax had become a source of revenue for the government, while saying the future direction of equity taxation remained uncertain.“We need to be mindful that, unlike many other economies that run surpluses, exporting more than they consume or producing more than they consume, India is much more dependent on foreign flows,” he said.He added that attracting foreign investment would remain important until India built sufficient manufacturing strength to export substantially more than it does today.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

Shah expects the resulting revenue growth to create operating leverage, with additional capital expenditure and expenses remaining relatively limited compared with the opportunity.India needs foreign investment until exports strengthenOn equity taxation, Shah said India needed to remain mindful of its dependence on foreign investment flows to fund its deficit.

Shah said the emerging weakness challenged the broader narrative that a massive AI build-out would eventually disrupt and wipe out several other industries.Anand Shah starts adding to IT stocks after prolonged underweight positionDespite concerns about AI disruption, Shah sees a potential opportunity for Indian IT services companies as businesses move towards integrating AI into their operations.ICICI Prudential AMC has started increasing its exposure to IT stocks after remaining underweight for a prolonged period, although the fund house will remain marginally underweight for now.“The next leg is when we will gain the confidence to increase our weightages,” Shah said.He said IT companies had been cutting prices and passing on a significant part of the benefits from AI to customers while still managing their top line. As companies seek to integrate AI into their systems, IT services providers could benefit from the implementation work. Greater confidence in the sector's performance could prompt the fund house to increase its allocation further.Why ICICI Prudential AMC prefers manufacturing stocksShah said ICICI Prudential AMC remained overweight on manufacturing across large-, mid- and small-cap stocks, pointing to improving earnings and a changing competitive environment for Indian businesses competing with China.He said Indian manufacturers had faced pressure from Chinese competition for 15-20 years, but the situation was changing at the margin. Measures in China to curb excessive competition had also contributed to price increases in sectors such as chemicals.Metals offered another indication of the opportunity, with earnings growth of more than 30% over the previous few quarters, according to Shah. He also highlighted strong cash-flow generation, while cautioning that metal stocks remained inherently cyclical and volatile.Indian metal companies could benefit from having costs in rupees and revenues linked to the dollar, alongside access to resources such as iron ore, bauxite and coal. Shah added that rupee depreciation against the Chinese yuan had created a tailwind for Indian manufacturers competing with China, while making Chinese goods and raw materials more expensive for Indian buyers.Consumer companies face rising costs and tougher competitionIn contrast to manufacturing, Shah said consumer-facing businesses were dealing with higher input costs and intensifying competition, making it harder for companies to protect profitability.He pointed to the paint industry, where the number of major players had increased from four to seven or eight. The transition from 4G to 5G has been slower than the earlier shift from 3G to 4G because fewer immediate use cases have developed, he said. Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology's growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google's parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google's AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company's money-maker. Google's Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It's spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, revenue grew 39%, Amazon's stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta s also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It's guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it's "very compute-intensive to run," CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn't an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It's worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn't just coming from the Big Tech companies' profits. It's also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. The Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.

Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.

Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.

Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week.

Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank .

It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.
Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.

These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.
