sources.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow - The Business Times
passages: The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

extraction.body: TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom. But now there is growing uncertainty around just how easily more money can be obtained – and how much of it will be paid back. Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave. Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations. Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s. At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI. The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive AI projects. The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out. Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines. The spread, or extra premium that investors demand to put their money into risky AI debt investments, has shot up more than 50 per cent over the past six months, according to Barclays, the investment bank. “The market is on a knife’s edge everywhere,” said Alexandra Coleman, founder of Azraq, a data centre risk researcher. A lot is riding on the continuation of the borrowing binge. Every week lately, economists, banks and private equity firms project higher and higher amounts of debt that they say will be needed to finance the AI systems that their boosters assert will run the world in a few years. Virtually every major mutual fund company, insurer and private equity firm has been buying up the AI debt, to say nothing of the scores of individual investors who have poured money into skyrocketing AI companies. Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally. The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals. Investors have also sold out of some these companies’ existing debt, though the drop in bond prices has been less steep than for CoreWeave. CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description. Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork. First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips. Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more. CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame. The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around. Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future. Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire. A CoreWeave spokesperson, Lia Davis, said the company disagreed with the WeWork comparison. “The complexity of our financing reflects discipline, which is a point of pride for us,” she said in a statement. Another worry is the growing number of US data-centre projects being delayed by permitting issues or, in some cases, falling through. Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects. In 2025, the company easily borrowed US$38 billion from a group of banks to build, with the help of project developers, a pair of data centres, one in Texas and another on about 809 hectares of farmland in Port Washington, Wisconsin. Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028. Aterio, a data centre researcher, said it was looking less likely that Project Lighthouse’s four data centres would start operating before 2029. That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due. Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan. Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico. The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power. Some of the US$18 billion in debt tied to the project has recently sold at steep discounts, roughly US$0.80 on the US dollar, according to two people familiar with the trades. SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI. The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more. To get that money, Son sold off most of SoftBank’s holdings of Nvidia and T-Mobile and took out loans against his stake in chip designer Arm Holdings. In 2026, Son invested again. On Oct 1, SoftBank completed another US$30 billion investment in OpenAI. Before doing so, in late September the company raised a record US$11 billion in debt at interest rates of nearly 10 per cent. In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed. “The assets we’ve owned have increased significantly,” Clavel said in an interview. The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked. It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt. At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000. Some investors see a potential silver lining to the troubles. John Lloyd, the global head of multisector and corporate credit at asset manager Janus Henderson, said slowing down the financing for projects “makes existing projects and existing AI infrastructure even more valuable.” NYTIMES

sources.title: AI spending is soaring, but where is the revenue? Anand Shah flags cracks in the boom
passages: Anand Shah, CIO of PMS & AIF at ICICI Prudential AMC, sees cracks emerging in the artificial intelligence investment boom as revenue generation fails to keep pace with spending on infrastructure.
He believes the sustainability of the massive investment cycle will depend on how effectively AI companies convert spending into revenue.“Today, the boom is in AI investment.

We are not seeing a big boom in terms of revenue,” Shah told CNBC-TV18 in an interview.He pointed to pressure on companies supplying AI infrastructure, including chip manufacturers and businesses benefiting from electrification, alongside revenue concerns among AI companies.

He argued that the country would continue to need foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investor flows unless exports increased significantly relative to imports.Shah also noted that the securities transaction tax had become a source of revenue for the government, while saying the future direction of equity taxation remained uncertain.“We need to be mindful that, unlike many other economies that run surpluses, exporting more than they consume or producing more than they consume, India is much more dependent on foreign flows,” he said.He added that attracting foreign investment would remain important until India built sufficient manufacturing strength to export substantially more than it does today.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

Shah expects the resulting revenue growth to create operating leverage, with additional capital expenditure and expenses remaining relatively limited compared with the opportunity.India needs foreign investment until exports strengthenOn equity taxation, Shah said India needed to remain mindful of its dependence on foreign investment flows to fund its deficit.

As companies seek to integrate AI into their systems, IT services providers could benefit from the implementation work. Greater confidence in the sector's performance could prompt the fund house to increase its allocation further.Why ICICI Prudential AMC prefers manufacturing stocksShah said ICICI Prudential AMC remained overweight on manufacturing across large-, mid- and small-cap stocks, pointing to improving earnings and a changing competitive environment for Indian businesses competing with China.He said Indian manufacturers had faced pressure from Chinese competition for 15-20 years, but the situation was changing at the margin. Measures in China to curb excessive competition had also contributed to price increases in sectors such as chemicals.Metals offered another indication of the opportunity, with earnings growth of more than 30% over the previous few quarters, according to Shah. He also highlighted strong cash-flow generation, while cautioning that metal stocks remained inherently cyclical and volatile.Indian metal companies could benefit from having costs in rupees and revenues linked to the dollar, alongside access to resources such as iron ore, bauxite and coal. Shah added that rupee depreciation against the Chinese yuan had created a tailwind for Indian manufacturers competing with China, while making Chinese goods and raw materials more expensive for Indian buyers.Consumer companies face rising costs and tougher competitionIn contrast to manufacturing, Shah said consumer-facing businesses were dealing with higher input costs and intensifying competition, making it harder for companies to protect profitability.He pointed to the paint industry, where the number of major players had increased from four to seven or eight. The transition from 4G to 5G has been slower than the earlier shift from 3G to 4G because fewer immediate use cases have developed, he said. He also highlighted strong cash-flow generation, while cautioning that metal stocks remained inherently cyclical and volatile.Indian metal companies could benefit from having costs in rupees and revenues linked to the dollar, alongside access to resources such as iron ore, bauxite and coal.

Shah added that rupee depreciation against the Chinese yuan had created a tailwind for Indian manufacturers competing with China, while making Chinese goods and raw materials more expensive for Indian buyers.Consumer companies face rising costs and tougher competitionIn contrast to manufacturing, Shah said consumer-facing businesses were dealing with higher input costs and intensifying competition, making it harder for companies to protect profitability.He pointed to the paint industry, where the number of major players had increased from four to seven or eight.
The transition from 4G to 5G has been slower than the earlier shift from 3G to 4G because fewer immediate use cases have developed, he said.

Shah expects the resulting revenue growth to create operating leverage, with additional capital expenditure and expenses remaining relatively limited compared with the opportunity.India needs foreign investment until exports strengthenOn equity taxation, Shah said India needed to remain mindful of its dependence on foreign investment flows to fund its deficit.

He argued that the country would continue to need foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investor flows unless exports increased significantly relative to imports.Shah also noted that the securities transaction tax had become a source of revenue for the government, while saying the future direction of equity taxation remained uncertain.“We need to be mindful that, unlike many other economies that run surpluses, exporting more than they consume or producing more than they consume, India is much more dependent on foreign flows,” he said.He added that attracting foreign investment would remain important until India built sufficient manufacturing strength to export substantially more than it does today.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

sources.title: Binance targeted in $6.3 billion crypto heist, the largest ever - Yahoo Finance
passages: The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars' worth of digital currencies on the exchange.
"The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B," Binance said late Thursday on X .
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.
Binance will "cover all losses" from the hack, it said, adding, "User funds are safe."
Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws.
President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon .

Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.

The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.

extraction.body: The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded. The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds. The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed "an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." "The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B," Binance said late Thursday on X . About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said. Binance will "cover all losses" from the hack, it said, adding, "User funds are safe." "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice," it said. Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars' worth of digital currencies on the exchange. Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges. The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025. Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change. " This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," it said. As word of the hack spread online Thursday, major cryptocurrencies traded lower. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value. Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them. Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X . Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement. The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence. Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers' personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million . Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests, instead. Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered." Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon . sources.title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’ - The Guardian
passages: The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.
North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered.
The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.
Q&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?
Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003 .
“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack”.
Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack?
Binance exchange says it will cover customer losses as it scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far
In a post on X, Binance reiterated that it was working “to trace, freeze and recover additional funds”, and signed off: “We will weather this storm.

coreStoryFacts.text: The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars' worth of digital currencies on the exchange.
"The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B," Binance said late Thursday on X .
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.
Binance will "cover all losses" from the hack, it said, adding, "User funds are safe."
Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws.
President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon .

Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.

The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, as did Elliptic and another research outfit, Chainalysis.
North Korea, a state hampered by sanctions and starved for cash, has become a prolific hacker of crypto, an asset it favours because it can be stolen in bulk and laundered.
The regime has stolen more than $6.5bn in crypto assets in recent years, including more than $1bn so far in 2026, according to Elliptic.
Q&A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?
Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003 .
“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic.

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and within hours bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – had fallen 5% from its level before news of the hack broke, to $77,380, its lowest level in six weeks.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.

While crypto companies are not regulated in the UK, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could hurt the UK’s wider financial system.

extraction.body: A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens. Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets , making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them. Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company . The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach. The company says it will cover customers' losses . Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds. For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back. Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026. But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses. In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed. Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024 . "When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it." When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated. U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database . Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company. Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk. In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers. "If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says. Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says. If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody." With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it. That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe. And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says. For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them. "Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says. sources.title: Binance targeted in $6.3 billion crypto heist, the largest ever
passages: The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.

The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X.
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.

Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws.

Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.

The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.

extraction.body: The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded. The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds. The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X. About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said. Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.” “We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said. Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange. Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges. The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025. Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change. “This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value. Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them. Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X. Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement. The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million. Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws.

sources.title: Binance's $6.3 billion hack: How crypto insurance works
passages: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance in the world's biggest crypto heist, highlighting how cryptocurrency exchanges insure their digital assets against theft and cyberattacks.However, insurance protection varies widely.

Binance established the Secure Asset Fund for Users in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect users in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents.As of 2026, the SAFU fund holds crypto assets worth roughly $1 billion, entirely in bitcoin, according to Binance's website.

While cyber policies can cover both first-party losses and third-party liabilities, including forensic investigations, customer notifications and legal expenses, they generally exclude the loss or transfer of funds.As a result, standalone cyber policies typically do not cover the full value of stolen cryptocurrency unless specific digital asset coverage has been added.How do insurers assess crypto theft claims?Insurers examine how a breach occurred, which systems were compromised and whether the resulting loss falls within the policy's coverage.They may also assess whether the exchange followed the required security procedures, including controls over private keys, wallet access and transaction approvals.The distinction between an external hacker stealing credentials and an employee deliberately transferring assets can determine whether a crime or cyber insurance policy covers the loss.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, was hit late Thursday by what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history , with $6.3 billion in funds impacted and roughly half of those assets frozen. Customer withdrawals have been temporarily suspended, and co-CEO Richard Teng promised the exchange will cover all losses. "We are committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds. Your assets are safe," Teng said on social media. Binance said it has money set aside in a Secure Asset Fund for Users to handle extreme cases, such as security breaches. Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post Friday morning that customer withdrawals should resume within 48 hours. "We are rebuilding the withdrawal service, and we are not switching it back until it passes rigorous testing," noted Teng on Friday. "We are very hopeful that users will be able to withdraw prior to the Sunday deadline." Teng said the hack was not carried out by one person. Initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but further review revealed broader security breaches. "This was a complex attack," Teng said. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers." The attack has rattled crypto markets and related stocks. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) tumbled 5% to hover below $77,000 on Friday. Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping 4% to around $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also plunged by more than 6%. Crypto-related stocks traded lower, led by shares of Circle, trading platforms Coinbase ( COIN ) and Robinhood ( HOOD ), and digital-asset Treasury giant Strategy ( MSTR ). Binance said that about $3 billion in assets have been "frozen on-chain so far." The frozen assets include over $2 billion in stablecoins. Tether, the world's largest stablecoin issuer, "froze more than 1.567B" of its USDT stablecoin in relation to the hack," CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X . The second-largest issuer, Circle ( CRCL ), froze another $800 million "in coordination with law enforcement," CEO Jeremy Allaire said. World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency venture co-founded by President Trump and his sons, said it froze $27 million of its stablecoin, USD1, associated with the hack, according to CEO Zack Witkoff. Although details are still emerging, the hack is shaping up to be the largest crypto theft in history, far exceeding the previous record set in February 2025, when attackers stole $1.5 billion from the crypto derivatives exchange ByBit. Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack. Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting for nearly all of those funds. The firm estimated that attackers still controlled over $3 billion in crypto that token issuers cannot directly freeze. The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance, in its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests the incident may have begun with a compromised engineer's laptop. The exchange added that it has found no evidence that wallet passwords were leaked. North Korean hackers swiped $2 billion in 2025 , bringing the rogue regime's total haul since 2016 through the end of last year to $6.75 billion, according to data from crypto firm Chainalysis. "This is likely the largest crypto hack on record, but the key distinction is that it does not currently appear to be a solvency event for Binance," Fundstrat head of digital assets Sean Farrell said. "That meaningfully reduces the risk of a negative feedback loop involving withdrawals, forced selling, tighter credit, and broader deleveraging," he added. Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, was hit late Thursday by what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history , with $6.3 billion in funds impacted and roughly half of those assets frozen.
Customer withdrawals have been temporarily suspended, and co-CEO Richard Teng promised the exchange will cover all losses.
"We are committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds. Your assets are safe," Teng said on social media.
Binance said it has money set aside in a Secure Asset Fund for Users to handle extreme cases, such as security breaches.
Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post Friday morning that customer withdrawals should resume within 48 hours.

"We are rebuilding the withdrawal service, and we are not switching it back until it passes rigorous testing," noted Teng on Friday. "We are very hopeful that users will be able to withdraw prior to the Sunday deadline."
Teng said the hack was not carried out by one person. Initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but further review revealed broader security breaches.
"This was a complex attack," Teng said. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers."
The attack has rattled crypto markets and related stocks. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) tumbled 5% to hover below $77,000 on Friday.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping 4% to around $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also plunged by more than 6%.
Crypto-related stocks traded lower, led by shares of Circle, trading platforms Coinbase ( COIN ) and Robinhood ( HOOD ), and digital-asset Treasury giant Strategy ( MSTR ).
Binance said that about $3 billion in assets have been "frozen on-chain so far."

The frozen assets include over $2 billion in stablecoins. Tether, the world's largest stablecoin issuer, "froze more than 1.567B" of its USDT stablecoin in relation to the hack," CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X . The second-largest issuer, Circle ( CRCL ), froze another $800 million "in coordination with law enforcement," CEO Jeremy Allaire said. World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency venture co-founded by President Trump and his sons, said it froze $27 million of its stablecoin, USD1, associated with the hack, according to CEO Zack Witkoff.

Although details are still emerging, the hack is shaping up to be the largest crypto theft in history, far exceeding the previous record set in February 2025, when attackers stole $1.5 billion from the crypto derivatives exchange ByBit.

Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack.

Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting for nearly all of those funds. The firm estimated that attackers still controlled over $3 billion in crypto that token issuers cannot directly freeze.

The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance, in its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests the incident may have begun with a compromised engineer's laptop. The exchange added that it has found no evidence that wallet passwords were leaked.
North Korean hackers swiped $2 billion in 2025 , bringing the rogue regime's total haul since 2016 through the end of last year to $6.75 billion, according to data from crypto firm Chainalysis.

"This is likely the largest crypto hack on record, but the key distinction is that it does not currently appear to be a solvency event for Binance," Fundstrat head of digital assets Sean Farrell said.
"That meaningfully reduces the risk of a negative feedback loop involving withdrawals, forced selling, tighter credit, and broader deleveraging," he added.

extraction.body: A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens. Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets , making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them. Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company . The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach. The company says it will cover customers' losses . Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds. For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back. Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026. But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses. In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed. Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024 . "When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it." When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated. U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database . Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company. Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk. In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers. "If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says. Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says. If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody." With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it. That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe. And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says. For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them. "Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says. sources.title: Binance targeted in $6.3 billion crypto heist, the largest ever
passages: The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.

The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X.
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.

Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws.

Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.

The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.

sources.title: Binance's $6.3 billion hack: How crypto insurance works
passages: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance in the world's biggest crypto heist, highlighting how cryptocurrency exchanges insure their digital assets against theft and cyberattacks.However, insurance protection varies widely.

Binance established the Secure Asset Fund for Users in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect users in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents.As of 2026, the SAFU fund holds crypto assets worth roughly $1 billion, entirely in bitcoin, according to Binance's website.

While cyber policies can cover both first-party losses and third-party liabilities, including forensic investigations, customer notifications and legal expenses, they generally exclude the loss or transfer of funds.As a result, standalone cyber policies typically do not cover the full value of stolen cryptocurrency unless specific digital asset coverage has been added.How do insurers assess crypto theft claims?Insurers examine how a breach occurred, which systems were compromised and whether the resulting loss falls within the policy's coverage.They may also assess whether the exchange followed the required security procedures, including controls over private keys, wallet access and transaction approvals.The distinction between an external hacker stealing credentials and an employee deliberately transferring assets can determine whether a crime or cyber insurance policy covers the loss.

Where losses exceed the insured amount, the company must rely on its own financial resources or other recovery arrangements to meet its obligations.Some exchanges also maintain reserve funds to reimburse customers following security breaches. Binance established the Secure Asset Fund for Users in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect users in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents.As of 2026, the SAFU fund holds crypto assets worth roughly $1 billion, entirely in bitcoin, according to Binance's website. The company did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment on its insurance coverage.What can prevent an insurance payout?Exclusions that allow insurers to deny certain claims are common in policies covering digital assets and the personal liabilities of directors and officers at cryptocurrency companies. These can limit the scope of protection available to companies and make it harder for them to secure coverage.Common exclusions in these policies include cryptocurrency price fluctuations, fraudulent acts by the policyholder and inadequate or negligent key management.Do traditional crime and cyber insurance policies cover crypto?Most standard crime insurance policies do not cover cryptocurrency losses, as they were originally designed to protect assets such as cash, securities and precious metals.Traditional cyber liability policies also do not always cover the value of digital assets stolen in a hack. extraction.body: A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens. Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets , making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them. Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company . The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach. The company says it will cover customers' losses . Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds. For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back. Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026. But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses. In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed. Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024 . "When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it." When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated. U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database . Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company. Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk. In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers. "If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says. Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says. If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody." With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it. That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe. And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says. For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them. "Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says. sources.title: What smart people are saying about the $6 billion Binance hack
passages: Here's what smart people are saying about the Binance breach.

After hackers stole more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from the exchange platform Binance on Thursday, crypto executives are racing to help the company while blockchain researchers examine the damage and assign blame.
Binance initially said one engineer's compromised laptop was the gateway to the attack, but the company later revised its assessment, saying the attack was broader in scope.
In a video posted to X on Friday, Richard Teng, the co-CEO of Binance, said the attacker employed a "self-destruct mechanism" to hide their tracks, making Binance's investigation more difficult.

passages: The first question that comes to mind after hearing that Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, was hacked to the tune of $6.2 billion is: How the heck can this even happen?The hack, which lasted several hours, saw the attacker drain Binance's wallets, with hundreds of millions of dollars in BTC, ETH, USDC, USDT, and other cryptocurrencies.
The total tally, according to Binance co-CEO Richard Tang, was $6.3 billion.
Crypto sleuth Wazz put it at $6.17 billion by following crypto wallets, and Binance founder Changpeng 'CZ' Zhao didn't share the actual number, but he did confirm the ballpark.
If a single compromised laptop can result in billions being stolen, Binance had better rethink its security practices.
The same group was named responsible by the FBI for the $1.5 billion attack on crypto exchange Bybit back in 2025.

So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," he wrote, adding that the company will share a "detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified - and publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete."Furthermore, according to the BBC, Binance has uncovered "additional points of breach," so it may not be just the one laptop that was compromised.

coreStoryFacts.text: Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets , making it the largest crypto hack on record.
Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them.
For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange.
While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back.
The company says it will cover customers' losses .
Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach.
Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026.

Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company .
FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says.
If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody."
Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it.
When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself.

The cryptocurrency exchange has temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals following an incident involving an estimated $6.3 billion in digital assets.Binance has said customer funds are safe and promised to cover the estimated losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company reserves.

Binance hack: The biggest concern for Binance users right now is not just how the reported security breach happened, but whether they can access their money.

The company says it will cover customers' losses . Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back. Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026. But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses. In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed. Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024 . "When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it." When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated. U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database . Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company. Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk. In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers. "If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says. Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says. If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody." With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it. That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe. And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says. For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them. "Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says. sources.title: What smart people are saying about the $6 billion Binance hack
passages: Here's what smart people are saying about the Binance breach.

After hackers stole more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from the exchange platform Binance on Thursday, crypto executives are racing to help the company while blockchain researchers examine the damage and assign blame.
Binance initially said one engineer's compromised laptop was the gateway to the attack, but the company later revised its assessment, saying the attack was broader in scope.
In a video posted to X on Friday, Richard Teng, the co-CEO of Binance, said the attacker employed a "self-destruct mechanism" to hide their tracks, making Binance's investigation more difficult.

The total tally, according to Binance co-CEO Richard Tang, was $6.3 billion.
Crypto sleuth Wazz put it at $6.17 billion by following crypto wallets, and Binance founder Changpeng 'CZ' Zhao didn't share the actual number, but he did confirm the ballpark.
If a single compromised laptop can result in billions being stolen, Binance had better rethink its security practices.
The same group was named responsible by the FBI for the $1.5 billion attack on crypto exchange Bybit back in 2025.

So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," he wrote, adding that the company will share a "detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified - and publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete."Furthermore, according to the BBC, Binance has uncovered "additional points of breach," so it may not be just the one laptop that was compromised.
CET Crypto analysis firm TRM claims with "high confidence" that the hack has been done by North Korea's "elite hacking unit" called TraderTraitor.
Fortunately for Binance and its users, a substantial portion of the stolen funds has been frozen by the issuers.

A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations. Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens. Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures. Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen. 2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance. Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up. The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. Protocols that are slower to respond may not be so lucky. The Binance theft came within hours of a separate, much smaller theft of around $2.7 million from Polymarket users [ W3IGG ], and some people wondered whether the two were connected. I doubt it. Polymarket has blamed its incident on a compromised third-party vendor, which an attacker apparently used to inject a malicious script into the site’s frontend and steal user funds. The Binance attacker got access to the exchange’s own hot wallets. They’re very different attacks, and nothing besides timing ties them together so far.
