These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations.

Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens.

Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion .

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”

He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.)

Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures.

Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen. 2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance.

Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up.

The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. Protocols that are slower to respond may not be so lucky.

passages: The Binance hack resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in crypto outflows across 10 blockchains.
Investigators believe a compromised DevOps laptop and an exploit involving Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality helped attackers drain exchange-controlled wallets.

extraction.body: The Binance hack resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in crypto outflows across 10 blockchains. Investigators believe a compromised DevOps laptop and an exploit involving Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality helped attackers drain exchange-controlled wallets. The Binance hack has emerged as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, after attackers moved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from wallets belonging to the world's largest crypto exchange. The incident, which occurred on October 29, 2026, involved unauthorized withdrawals across 10 blockchain networks and may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to a Binance DevOps engineer. Binance's preliminary investigation suggests the attacker used the compromised device to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in outflows and attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group. The investigation also revealed that attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality to gain control over a hot wallet's transaction execution. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in assets and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the attack. According to the exchange, the attacker used access from the compromised device to reach an internal service container. This container reportedly provided a route to systems involved in processing withdrawal transactions. Instead of directly stealing wallet private keys, the attackers allegedly exploited the infrastructure responsible for authorizing transactions. This distinction is important. Cryptocurrency exchanges use hot wallets to process withdrawals, and these wallets must interact with internal applications and transaction-signing systems. If an attacker gains control over an application or service authorized to request transactions, they may be able to move funds without extracting the underlying private keys. Binance said its investigation found no evidence of a private-key leak. However, the exchange has not yet published a complete technical post-mortem explaining exactly how the laptop was compromised or how the attacker gained access to the internal signing infrastructure. One of the most significant findings from the blockchain investigation concerns Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality. Introduced through Ethereum's Pectra upgrade, EIP-7702 allows externally owned accounts to temporarily delegate transaction execution to smart-contract code through signed authorizations. TRM Labs reported that the attacker used this mechanism to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper account controlled by the attacker. The process involved 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. Each authorization corresponded to a different transaction nonce, which determines the sequence of transactions from an Ethereum account. More importantly, the delegation remained active. As additional funds arrived in the Binance hot wallet, the attacker could execute further transfers instead of relying on a single withdrawal. TRM Labs reported that the wallet was swept multiple times. The attacker also used the compromised wallet's execution capabilities to access funds associated with a separate Binance smart account. This method allowed the attackers to exploit transaction authorization rather than directly extracting the wallet's private key. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in transfers from Binance-attributed wallets across 10 blockchain networks. According to TRM Labs, most of the initial outflows happened within approximately 20 minutes, beginning at 20:05 UTC on October 29. A later wave of transactions involved wallets on Avalanche and Polygon. Ethereum accounted for the largest share of the reported outflows, with approximately $3.79 billion in assets transferred. Bitcoin outflows reached approximately 18,270 BTC, worth around $1.47 billion at the time of the transfers. The attackers also moved substantial quantities of stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, alongside other digital assets. The activity across multiple networks suggests that the incident involved more than an isolated Ethereum wallet exploit. TRM Labs believes the attackers gained access to Binance's broader hot-wallet signing infrastructure, although the exchange has yet to confirm the complete technical explanation. After draining the wallets, the attackers began moving and converting the stolen assets to make recovery more difficult. Binance worked with blockchain intelligence firms, stablecoin issuers, and other industry participants to limit the movement of stolen funds. The exchange initially reported that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. TRM Labs separately estimated that around $2.7 billion in assets had been frozen through stablecoin issuers and blockchain-level interventions at the time of its analysis. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial participated in freezing affected stablecoins. Arbitrum's Security Council also froze assets on its network. Despite these interventions, TRM Labs estimated that the attacker still controlled more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion at the time of its analysis. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals across several networks while conducting security checks and coordinating with its partners. The response highlights the importance of emergency reserves in centralized exchange security. TRM Labs attributed the Binance hack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking unit. The firm's assessment was based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence, as well as similarities between this incident and previous attacks associated with the group. Chainalysis also reportedly linked the attack to North Korean hackers. However, Binance has not officially identified the attackers, and the attribution remains an assessment by blockchain intelligence firms rather than a publicly confirmed government finding. TraderTraitor has previously been associated with major cryptocurrency thefts, including the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." "An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said.
What is TraderTraitor?In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit.

The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.Working "around the clock" Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017.

This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft.

What is TraderTraitor?In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said. "An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.Working "around the clock" Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties. In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world. Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered." The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab. "This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet. Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

extraction.body: Stablecoin issuers froze about $2.4 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen. The rest exceeds Binance’s insurance fund, and the man promising to make users whole isn’t supposed to be running the company. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations. Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens. Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures. Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen. 2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance. Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up. The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. Protocols that are slower to respond may not be so lucky. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations.

Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens.

Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion .

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”

He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.)

Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures.

This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. Protocols that are slower to respond may not be so lucky.

Polymarket has blamed its incident on a compromised third-party vendor, which an attacker apparently used to inject a malicious script into the site’s frontend and steal user funds. The Binance attacker got access to the exchange’s own hot wallets. They’re very different attacks, and nothing besides timing ties them together so far.

extraction.body: The Binance hack resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in crypto outflows across 10 blockchains. Investigators believe a compromised DevOps laptop and an exploit involving Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality helped attackers drain exchange-controlled wallets. The Binance hack has emerged as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, after attackers moved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from wallets belonging to the world's largest crypto exchange. The incident, which occurred on October 29, 2026, involved unauthorized withdrawals across 10 blockchain networks and may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to a Binance DevOps engineer. Binance's preliminary investigation suggests the attacker used the compromised device to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in outflows and attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group. The investigation also revealed that attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality to gain control over a hot wallet's transaction execution. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in assets and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the attack. According to the exchange, the attacker used access from the compromised device to reach an internal service container. This container reportedly provided a route to systems involved in processing withdrawal transactions. Instead of directly stealing wallet private keys, the attackers allegedly exploited the infrastructure responsible for authorizing transactions. This distinction is important. Cryptocurrency exchanges use hot wallets to process withdrawals, and these wallets must interact with internal applications and transaction-signing systems. If an attacker gains control over an application or service authorized to request transactions, they may be able to move funds without extracting the underlying private keys. Binance said its investigation found no evidence of a private-key leak. However, the exchange has not yet published a complete technical post-mortem explaining exactly how the laptop was compromised or how the attacker gained access to the internal signing infrastructure. One of the most significant findings from the blockchain investigation concerns Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality. Introduced through Ethereum's Pectra upgrade, EIP-7702 allows externally owned accounts to temporarily delegate transaction execution to smart-contract code through signed authorizations. TRM Labs reported that the attacker used this mechanism to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper account controlled by the attacker. The process involved 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. Each authorization corresponded to a different transaction nonce, which determines the sequence of transactions from an Ethereum account. More importantly, the delegation remained active. As additional funds arrived in the Binance hot wallet, the attacker could execute further transfers instead of relying on a single withdrawal. TRM Labs reported that the wallet was swept multiple times. The attacker also used the compromised wallet's execution capabilities to access funds associated with a separate Binance smart account. This method allowed the attackers to exploit transaction authorization rather than directly extracting the wallet's private key. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in transfers from Binance-attributed wallets across 10 blockchain networks. According to TRM Labs, most of the initial outflows happened within approximately 20 minutes, beginning at 20:05 UTC on October 29. A later wave of transactions involved wallets on Avalanche and Polygon. Ethereum accounted for the largest share of the reported outflows, with approximately $3.79 billion in assets transferred. Bitcoin outflows reached approximately 18,270 BTC, worth around $1.47 billion at the time of the transfers. The attackers also moved substantial quantities of stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, alongside other digital assets. The activity across multiple networks suggests that the incident involved more than an isolated Ethereum wallet exploit. TRM Labs believes the attackers gained access to Binance's broader hot-wallet signing infrastructure, although the exchange has yet to confirm the complete technical explanation. After draining the wallets, the attackers began moving and converting the stolen assets to make recovery more difficult. Binance worked with blockchain intelligence firms, stablecoin issuers, and other industry participants to limit the movement of stolen funds. The exchange initially reported that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. TRM Labs separately estimated that around $2.7 billion in assets had been frozen through stablecoin issuers and blockchain-level interventions at the time of its analysis. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial participated in freezing affected stablecoins. Arbitrum's Security Council also froze assets on its network. Despite these interventions, TRM Labs estimated that the attacker still controlled more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion at the time of its analysis. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals across several networks while conducting security checks and coordinating with its partners. The response highlights the importance of emergency reserves in centralized exchange security. TRM Labs attributed the Binance hack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking unit. The firm's assessment was based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence, as well as similarities between this incident and previous attacks associated with the group. Chainalysis also reportedly linked the attack to North Korean hackers. However, Binance has not officially identified the attackers, and the attribution remains an assessment by blockchain intelligence firms rather than a publicly confirmed government finding. TraderTraitor has previously been associated with major cryptocurrency thefts, including the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations. Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens. Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures. Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up. The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. The Binance attacker got access to the exchange’s own hot wallets. They’re very different attacks, and nothing besides timing ties them together so far. Binance's preliminary investigation suggests the attacker used the compromised device to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in outflows and attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group. The investigation also revealed that attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality to gain control over a hot wallet's transaction execution. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in assets and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the attack. According to the exchange, the attacker used access from the compromised device to reach an internal service container. This container reportedly provided a route to systems involved in processing withdrawal transactions. Instead of directly stealing wallet private keys, the attackers allegedly exploited the infrastructure responsible for authorizing transactions. This distinction is important. Cryptocurrency exchanges use hot wallets to process withdrawals, and these wallets must interact with internal applications and transaction-signing systems. If an attacker gains control over an application or service authorized to request transactions, they may be able to move funds without extracting the underlying private keys. Binance said its investigation found no evidence of a private-key leak. However, the exchange has not yet published a complete technical post-mortem explaining exactly how the laptop was compromised or how the attacker gained access to the internal signing infrastructure. One of the most significant findings from the blockchain investigation concerns Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality. Introduced through Ethereum's Pectra upgrade, EIP-7702 allows externally owned accounts to temporarily delegate transaction execution to smart-contract code through signed authorizations. TRM Labs reported that the attacker used this mechanism to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper account controlled by the attacker. The process involved 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. Each authorization corresponded to a different transaction nonce, which determines the sequence of transactions from an Ethereum account. More importantly, the delegation remained active. As additional funds arrived in the Binance hot wallet, the attacker could execute further transfers instead of relying on a single withdrawal. TRM Labs reported that the wallet was swept multiple times. The attacker also used the compromised wallet's execution capabilities to access funds associated with a separate Binance smart account. This method allowed the attackers to exploit transaction authorization rather than directly extracting the wallet's private key. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in transfers from Binance-attributed wallets across 10 blockchain networks. According to TRM Labs, most of the initial outflows happened within approximately 20 minutes, beginning at 20:05 UTC on October 29. A later wave of transactions involved wallets on Avalanche and Polygon. Ethereum accounted for the largest share of the reported outflows, with approximately $3.79 billion in assets transferred. Bitcoin outflows reached approximately 18,270 BTC, worth around $1.47 billion at the time of the transfers. The attackers also moved substantial quantities of stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, alongside other digital assets. The activity across multiple networks suggests that the incident involved more than an isolated Ethereum wallet exploit. TRM Labs believes the attackers gained access to Binance's broader hot-wallet signing infrastructure, although the exchange has yet to confirm the complete technical explanation. After draining the wallets, the attackers began moving and converting the stolen assets to make recovery more difficult. Binance worked with blockchain intelligence firms, stablecoin issuers, and other industry participants to limit the movement of stolen funds. The exchange initially reported that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. TRM Labs separately estimated that around $2.7 billion in assets had been frozen through stablecoin issuers and blockchain-level interventions at the time of its analysis. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial participated in freezing affected stablecoins. Arbitrum's Security Council also froze assets on its network. Despite these interventions, TRM Labs estimated that the attacker still controlled more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion at the time of its analysis. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals across several networks while conducting security checks and coordinating with its partners. The response highlights the importance of emergency reserves in centralized exchange security. TRM Labs attributed the Binance hack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking unit. The firm's assessment was based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence, as well as similarities between this incident and previous attacks associated with the group. Chainalysis also reportedly linked the attack to North Korean hackers. However, Binance has not officially identified the attackers, and the attribution remains an assessment by blockchain intelligence firms rather than a publicly confirmed government finding. TraderTraitor has previously been associated with major cryptocurrency thefts, including the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025. coreStoryFacts.text: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two.

The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.

We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said.
What is TraderTraitor?In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit.

The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.Working "around the clock" Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017.

A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could.

These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations.
This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft.
I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up.

Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen.

2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance.

At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets.
The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion .
Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters.

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said.
What is TraderTraitor?In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017.

A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could.

These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations.
This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft.
I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up.

2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance.

At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets.
The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion .
Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters.

The exchange initially reported that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain.

A US-based blockchain intelligence firm called TRM Labs pinned the attack on TraderTraitor which is a North Korean hacking unit.
An insider called it “the largest bank heist in human history,” according to the New York Post.
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM stated.

extraction.body: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever. What is TraderTraitor?In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said. "An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.Working "around the clock" Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties. In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world. Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered." The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab. "This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet. Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

extraction.body: Stablecoin issuers froze about $2.4 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen. The rest exceeds Binance’s insurance fund, and the man promising to make users whole isn’t supposed to be running the company. A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations. Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens. Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion . Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.” He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.) Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures. Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen. 2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance. Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up. The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. Protocols that are slower to respond may not be so lucky. The Binance theft came within hours of a separate, much smaller theft of around $2.7 million from Polymarket users [ W3IGG ], and some people wondered whether the two were connected. I doubt it. Polymarket has blamed its incident on a compromised third-party vendor, which an attacker apparently used to inject a malicious script into the site’s frontend and steal user funds. The Binance attacker got access to the exchange’s own hot wallets. They’re very different attacks, and nothing besides timing ties them together so far. October 29 at 8:47pm: Updated to remove some skepticism around whether bitcoin attributed to the attacker was stolen, after a conversation with another researcher made me less confident the wallets were unrelated. October 30 at 1:17am: Updated with a statement from Binance and the report from TRM Labs. October 30 at 1:05pm: Updated with a link to my primer on North Korean crypto thefts , and with a revised total theft estimate from outside blockchain analytics firms. Exchanges hold most customer funds in “cold” wallets, more secure crypto wallets whose keys are kept offline and where assets are hard to move quickly. A smaller portion sits in “hot” wallets, whose keys are kept on internet-connected systems so the exchange can process withdrawals automatically. ↩ Binance insurance fund balance , Binance.com. ↩ " North Korea Steals USD 6.36 Billion From Binance in the Largest Hack in History , TRM Labs. ↩ Have information? passages: Stablecoin issuers froze about $2.4 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen. The rest exceeds Binance’s insurance fund, and the man promising to make users whole isn’t supposed to be running the company.

A notorious North Korean cybercrime group has stolen around $6.4 billion in cryptoassets from multiple hot wallets a belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and still controls around $3 billion of it after stablecoin issuers and other protocols froze what they could. These estimates are still in flux as various platforms work to freeze tokens or otherwise thwart the attacker from cashing out, and as both Binance and independent security researchers continue their investigations.

Unlike many supposedly “multi-billion dollar” crypto hacks, where the headline figure relies on the notional value of illiquid assets that could never be sold for anywhere near that amount, the majority of these stolen assets were major stablecoins, bitcoin, ethereum, and other fairly liquid tokens.

Binance has estimated the total theft at $6.3 billion; external estimates later revised the total up to around $6.4 billion. At least $5.5 billion of these were liquid assets. Tether announced they had frozen at least $1.567 billion of the stolen USDT, and Circle has frozen around $800 million of stolen USDC. World Liberty Financial froze the $27 million in USD1 stolen by the attacker, and the Arbitrum ethereum layer-2 network froze an additional $30.5 million that had moved to its network. The attacker is estimated to have made off with between $2.4 billion and $3.4 billion .

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who is legally not allowed to have any active role with the company [ I98 ] yet still has remarkable amounts of inside knowledge into its inner workings, posted on Twitter less than an hour after the theft that “User funds are safe!”, adding early estimates of how much Tether and Circle had frozen. He added, “I don't manage Binance (.com) anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”

He later tweeted “Loss might be a bit higher than [$1 billion], but will cover.” (Why a person who is barred from any control over Binance would be the one promising this is an exercise I will leave to the reader.)

Binance keeps an emergency insurance fund in case of exploits or other crypto disasters. Its most recent balance report puts it at around $1.3 billion. 1 Unless more is recovered, Binance will either fail to make users whole or dip into its own balance sheet — potentially to the tune of 10 figures.

Binance later wrote that their "initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop", which allowed an attacker to “submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” They estimated the total theft at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion frozen. 2 While the assets frozen by Tether and Circle will likely easily be returned to Binance, other non-centralized assets frozen by various protocols may be inaccessible both to the attacker and to Binance.

Blockchain security firm TRM Labs has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group. 3 The group has been linked to other massive cryptocurrency heists, including a massive $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit cryptocurrency exchange in 2025 [ W3IGG ]. This Binance hack has now surpassed the Bybit hack for the largest cryptocurrency theft. I’ve written more about North Korea’s crypto thefts, how they launder the funds, and what the money pays for in a follow-up.

The contagion also threatens to spread beyond Binance. Aave, a defi lending project, paused some of its markets to stop the attacker from depositing stolen assets as collateral and borrowing against them — a move that could otherwise leave it holding significant bad debt. Protocols that are slower to respond may not be so lucky.

The Binance theft came within hours of a separate, much smaller theft of around $2.7 million from Polymarket users [ W3IGG ], and some people wondered whether the two were connected. I doubt it. Polymarket has blamed its incident on a compromised third-party vendor, which an attacker apparently used to inject a malicious script into the site’s frontend and steal user funds. The Binance attacker got access to the exchange’s own hot wallets. They’re very different attacks, and nothing besides timing ties them together so far.

extraction.body: The Binance hack resulted in approximately $6.3 billion in crypto outflows across 10 blockchains. Investigators believe a compromised DevOps laptop and an exploit involving Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality helped attackers drain exchange-controlled wallets. The Binance hack has emerged as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, after attackers moved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from wallets belonging to the world's largest crypto exchange. The incident, which occurred on October 29, 2026, involved unauthorized withdrawals across 10 blockchain networks and may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to a Binance DevOps engineer. Binance's preliminary investigation suggests the attacker used the compromised device to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in outflows and attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group. The investigation also revealed that attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality to gain control over a hot wallet's transaction execution. Binance said it had worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in assets and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Binance's initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the attack. According to the exchange, the attacker used access from the compromised device to reach an internal service container. This container reportedly provided a route to systems involved in processing withdrawal transactions. Instead of directly stealing wallet private keys, the attackers allegedly exploited the infrastructure responsible for authorizing transactions. This distinction is important. Cryptocurrency exchanges use hot wallets to process withdrawals, and these wallets must interact with internal applications and transaction-signing systems. If an attacker gains control over an application or service authorized to request transactions, they may be able to move funds without extracting the underlying private keys. Binance said its investigation found no evidence of a private-key leak. However, the exchange has not yet published a complete technical post-mortem explaining exactly how the laptop was compromised or how the attacker gained access to the internal signing infrastructure. One of the most significant findings from the blockchain investigation concerns Ethereum's EIP-7702 functionality. Introduced through Ethereum's Pectra upgrade, EIP-7702 allows externally owned accounts to temporarily delegate transaction execution to smart-contract code through signed authorizations. TRM Labs reported that the attacker used this mechanism to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper account controlled by the attacker. The process involved 50 pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. Each authorization corresponded to a different transaction nonce, which determines the sequence of transactions from an Ethereum account. More importantly, the delegation remained active. As additional funds arrived in the Binance hot wallet, the attacker could execute further transfers instead of relying on a single withdrawal. TRM Labs reported that the wallet was swept multiple times. The attacker also used the compromised wallet's execution capabilities to access funds associated with a separate Binance smart account. This method allowed the attackers to exploit transaction authorization rather than directly extracting the wallet's private key. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. TRM Labs traced approximately $6.36 billion in transfers from Binance-attributed wallets across 10 blockchain networks. According to TRM Labs, most of the initial outflows happened within approximately 20 minutes, beginning at 20:05 UTC on October 29. A later wave of transactions involved wallets on Avalanche and Polygon. Ethereum accounted for the largest share of the reported outflows, with approximately $3.79 billion in assets transferred. Bitcoin outflows reached approximately 18,270 BTC, worth around $1.47 billion at the time of the transfers. The attackers also moved substantial quantities of stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, alongside other digital assets. The activity across multiple networks suggests that the incident involved more than an isolated Ethereum wallet exploit. TRM Labs believes the attackers gained access to Binance's broader hot-wallet signing infrastructure, although the exchange has yet to confirm the complete technical explanation. After draining the wallets, the attackers began moving and converting the stolen assets to make recovery more difficult. Binance worked with blockchain intelligence firms, stablecoin issuers, and other industry participants to limit the movement of stolen funds. The exchange initially reported that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. TRM Labs separately estimated that around $2.7 billion in assets had been frozen through stablecoin issuers and blockchain-level interventions at the time of its analysis. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial participated in freezing affected stablecoins. Arbitrum's Security Council also froze assets on its network. Despite these interventions, TRM Labs estimated that the attacker still controlled more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth approximately $2.4 billion at the time of its analysis. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals across several networks while conducting security checks and coordinating with its partners. The response highlights the importance of emergency reserves in centralized exchange security. TRM Labs attributed the Binance hack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking unit. The firm's assessment was based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence, as well as similarities between this incident and previous attacks associated with the group. Chainalysis also reportedly linked the attack to North Korean hackers. However, Binance has not officially identified the attackers, and the attribution remains an assessment by blockchain intelligence firms rather than a publicly confirmed government finding. TraderTraitor has previously been associated with major cryptocurrency thefts, including the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025. extraction.body: The United States ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia effective October 23 due to safety risks, the US embassy in Riyadh said on Friday, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure. US government employees require special authorization to use Saudi airports following recent missile and drone attacks, the embassy said, warning US citizens of potential further attacks, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions. The fighting between Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has intensified in recent weeks, opening a volatile new front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran. Yemen's government armed forces spokesperson said that the Houthis attacked Aden airport and the Maashiq presidential palace complex with ballistic missiles. The statement did not give details on any casualties, damage, or whether the missiles hit their intended targets. The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen also said it had intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis over Saudi Arabia 's Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest sites and visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims each year. passages: Prime Video, Amazon’s streaming service, “has emerged as a significant business with a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars and is now profitable in its own right,” Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on the quarterly earnings call on Thursday.
Prime Video broadcasts NASCAR, the Masters, and UEFA Champions League soccer, but Thursday Night Football appears to be its biggest success this year.

It’s been four years since Amazon bought MGM for $8.5 billion .
But coming off the blockbuster success of this year’s hit movie “Project Hail Mary,” Hollywood has become a lucrative business for the e-commerce giant.

coreStoryFacts.text: Prime Video, Amazon’s streaming service, “has emerged as a significant business with a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars and is now profitable in its own right,” Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on the quarterly earnings call on Thursday.
Prime Video broadcasts NASCAR, the Masters, and UEFA Champions League soccer, but Thursday Night Football appears to be its biggest success this year.
The first six games of this season have averaged 17.7 million viewers, up 16% from last year, according to Nielsen figures Amazon shared.
The streaming service also attracted over 2 million viewers for its second season of the NBA on Prime, Nielsen said.

Jassy also named a number of TV shows as hits, including “Carrie,” “The Summer I Turned Pretty,” “The Boys,” “Off Campus,” “Fallout,” and “Reacher.” Season 4 of “Reacher” drew 66 million viewers globally in its first 28 days, the company says, with more to come.
It’s been four years since Amazon bought MGM for $8.5 billion .
But coming off the blockbuster success of this year’s hit movie “Project Hail Mary,” Hollywood has become a lucrative business for the e-commerce giant.

extraction.body: It’s been four years since Amazon bought MGM for $8.5 billion . But coming off the blockbuster success of this year’s hit movie “Project Hail Mary,” Hollywood has become a lucrative business for the e-commerce giant. Prime Video, Amazon’s streaming service, “has emerged as a significant business with a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars and is now profitable in its own right,” Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on the quarterly earnings call on Thursday. Jassy had previously told investors in May that Prime Video was profitable , but being on track to generate tens of billions is a new detail. Amazon said its movie studio, Amazon MGM Studios, has brought in more than $1.2 billion in global box office sales so far this year, helped by hits like “Project Hail Mary” and “Verity.” “Project Hail Mary” grossed an estimated $684 million worldwide, according to The Numbers . Starring Ryan Gosling and based on Andy Weir’s novel , the film opened in theaters in March and became Amazon MGM Studios’ highest-grossing release, according to entertainment reports. (The studio also had at least one notable flop this year: “Melania.” ) Jassy also named a number of TV shows as hits, including “Carrie,” “The Summer I Turned Pretty,” “The Boys,” “Off Campus,” “Fallout,” and “Reacher.” Season 4 of “Reacher” drew 66 million viewers globally in its first 28 days, the company says, with more to come. Season 5 is filming now, and the show was picked up for a sixth season. (And if you don’t follow Alan Ritchson, the star of “Reacher,” on Threads, you are missing out on an actor who has turned a friendly-yet-witty reply into an art form.) Sports have also been a significant driver. Prime Video broadcasts NASCAR, the Masters, and UEFA Champions League soccer, but Thursday Night Football appears to be its biggest success this year. The first six games of this season have averaged 17.7 million viewers, up 16% from last year, according to Nielsen figures Amazon shared. The streaming service also attracted over 2 million viewers for its second season of the NBA on Prime, Nielsen said. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . passages: Binance halted trading Thursday after hackers allegedly linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion, the largest crypto hack in history.
The big picture: If estimates hold up, the Binance hack would be the biggest crypto attack in history.
Driving the news: Binance co-founder Yi He said on X that the crypto exchange had suspended deposits and withdrawals.
Binance's size makes it more insulated, March said.
"If this happened to any other business in crypto other than Binance, it would've been catastrophic."
An estimated $6.3 billion were drained from wallets in the incident, Binance said , although the exchange and partners managed to freeze about $3 billion that can potentially be recovered.
An initial investigation linked the hack to a compromised laptop from one Binance engineer.
That access allowed an attacker to gain access to Binance's systems to make withdrawals, the exchange said.
Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from Binance and findings of security researchers.
Representatives of North Korea have previously denied allegations of hacking crypto exchanges.
The country has turned hacking and scams into an industrial-scale scourge, focusing on crypto heists and a widespread practice of tricking Western companies into hiring North Korean workers .

extraction.body: Binance halted trading Thursday after hackers allegedly linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion, the largest crypto hack in history. Why it matters : The attack comes after a wave of high-profile cyber intrusions and data breaches during "Black October," when a series of security incidents and AI -discovered bugs triggered fears of a global crisis. Driving the news: Binance co-founder Yi He said on X that the crypto exchange had suspended deposits and withdrawals. "User funds are safe," she wrote. "Binance will cover all hacking losses." An estimated $6.3 billion were drained from wallets in the incident, Binance said , although the exchange and partners managed to freeze about $3 billion that can potentially be recovered. "This is unprecedented," said Kevin March, a co-founder of JPEG Trading, a cryptocurrency trading firm that closely tracked the hack to monitor market conditions. An initial investigation linked the hack to a compromised laptop from one Binance engineer. That access allowed an attacker to gain access to Binance's systems to make withdrawals, the exchange said. Zoom in: Researchers from TRM Labs and Pangolin Intelligence found that the attack appeared to be the work of a North Korean hacking collective. "This was absolutely North Korea," Nick Carlsen, a senior TRM investigator, told the Wall Street Journal . Representatives of North Korea have previously denied allegations of hacking crypto exchanges. The country has turned hacking and scams into an industrial-scale scourge, focusing on crypto heists and a widespread practice of tricking Western companies into hiring North Korean workers . A Binance spokesperson said the exchange's security teams are "reviewing all relevant information with urgency." The big picture: If estimates hold up, the Binance hack would be the biggest crypto attack in history. In 2025, North Korea-linked hackers stole about $1.5 billion worth of crypto from the Bybit exchange. Between the lines: Crypto is a relatively common hacking target, but massive attacks can leave smaller exchanges vulnerable to collapse due to the potential for panicked withdrawals. Binance's size makes it more insulated, March said. "If this happened to any other business in crypto other than Binance, it would've been catastrophic." The exchange is capable of covering potential losses through its insurance and balance sheet, he said, although broad reverberations in crypto markets and prices remain possible. The intrigue: Reports of a breach came just hours after Polymarket confirmed it was facing a cyberattack, prompting the decentralized prediction market operator to pause trading for an hour after an attacker made off with at least $2.7 million in user funds. Researchers at Hudson Rock tied the Polymarket incident to a breach involving third-party website monitoring tool DebugBear , which said earlier Thursday it was responding to its own security incident. What to watch: Binance has yet to confirm who may be behind the attack and the total value of the currencies suspected hackers made off with. sources.title: Binance estimates $6.3 billion hacked in crypto’s biggest heist - BusinessWorld Online
passages: Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, said $6.3 billion of funds are involved in what the industry is describing as crypto’s biggest-ever hack.
Before now, the biggest publicly known crypto hack occurred at exchange Bybit in February 2025, in which attackers made off with almost $1.5 billion of tokens.
For crypto faithful who’d been basking in a two-month-long price rebound, the Binance incident is a potential setback.
The two biggest stablecoin issuers said they took steps to freeze missing currency.
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said in a post on X.
“We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far.”
“The rumored Binance hack is definitely driving down coin prices,” said Fredrick Collins, chief executive and co-founder of crypto data platform Velo Data.

“Binance is such a behemoth in crypto that any hit to confidence in them is a hit to confidence in the industry as a whole, especially as people have already been skittish over the increasing cyber capabilities of AI.”

An emergency insurance and reserve fund from Binance called the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) was established in 2018 to serve a backstop for customers in “extreme situations,” according to the exchange.
The company said it will cover all losses and “user funds are safe.”
The hackers appear to have exploited how Binance authorizes transactions, according to TRM.
Binance said the incident may involve a compromised software engineer’s laptop.
Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs said North Korea was behind the heist, which it called “the largest crypto theft on record.”
