extraction.body: Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, said $6.3 billion of funds are involved in what the industry is describing as crypto’s biggest-ever hack. Digital tokens fell. “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said in a post on X. “We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far.” Binance has temporarily suspended all withdrawals, which it expects to resume within 48 hours, co-founder Yi He said in a post on X. The company said it will cover all losses and “user funds are safe.” Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs said North Korea was behind the heist, which it called “the largest crypto theft on record.” “TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” the firm said. “We make this judgment with high confidence.” Before now, the biggest publicly known crypto hack occurred at exchange Bybit in February 2025, in which attackers made off with almost $1.5 billion of tokens. For crypto faithful who’d been basking in a two-month-long price rebound, the Binance incident is a potential setback. Notorious previous episodes of theft and fraud among fallen crypto giants such as FTX and Mt. Gox set the stage for protracted bear markets, bruises the industry has worked to put behind it in US President Donald Trump’s promised new era of regulatory clarity for cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin dropped 3% at the end of the US session and a further 3% in Asia trading, falling below $77,000 to its lowest level since September, with other tokens also selling off. “The rumored Binance hack is definitely driving down coin prices,” said Fredrick Collins, chief executive and co-founder of crypto data platform Velo Data. “Binance is such a behemoth in crypto that any hit to confidence in them is a hit to confidence in the industry as a whole, especially as people have already been skittish over the increasing cyber capabilities of AI.” The hackers appear to have exploited how Binance authorizes transactions, according to TRM. They seemingly gained access to the exchange’s systems and used internal software to authorize transfers across 10 different blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, it said. Binance said the incident may involve a compromised software engineer’s laptop. “We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak,” the company said. An emergency insurance and reserve fund from Binance called the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) was established in 2018 to serve a backstop for customers in “extreme situations,” according to the exchange. The SAFU is generally maintained at around $1 billion, but has fluctuated in the past in tandem with market movements, Binance said in 2024. The two biggest stablecoin issuers said they took steps to freeze missing currency. Paolo Ardoino, the chief executive officer of Tether, said in an X post that it froze more than $1.5 billion of the stablecoin “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.” Jeremy Allaire, who runs Circle Internet Group Inc., said $800 million of its coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit involving Binance.” Sentiment was already fragile after a spate of crypto security incidents. In recent months, hundreds of millions of dollars were drained from Bitget, while tampering tied to Ledger devices also led to millions of dollars in losses. “Attackers are operating at unprecedented speed and scale” but “the tools to track and trace operate at that speed too,” said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “Stablecoin issuers freeze within hours. Investigators follow funds across chains in real time.” Traders had already been bracing for greater volatility in the crypto market this week, with $11 billion in options set to expire Friday. This comes days ahead of the US midterm elections taking place next week, when Democrats could potentially retake one or both chambers of Congress and open the door to greater regulatory scrutiny for the industry. Exchange thefts and malfeasance have been an ever-present backdrop of crypto’s almost two-decade ascent, the most famous of which was the collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX in November 2022. In what remains perhaps the most notorious hacking incident, Japan-based Bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was struck in 2011. Over time, the hackers made off with tokens worth billions of dollars based on the current market price. Mt. Gox eventually went bankrupt. “It’s a huge damage to crypto because of the consistent successful hacks in the space,” said Tian Zeng, chief executive officer of crypto hedge fund Third Eye. “The fact that exploits keep happening makes it dangerous in the age of newest AI models being released every two weeks.” The Binance incident came on the same day event-contract venue Polymarket halted trading on its international exchange for an hour after it said that a third-party software provider was compromised. More than 700 Polymarket users were drained of $2.7 million in funds, said blockchain analytics platform Bubblemaps, in a post on X. A spokesman declined to comment on the numbers. Recent security incidents haven’t been confined to crypto firms. South Korea’s Daishin Securities disclosed a data leak affecting about 38,000 customers this week, and Mirae Asset Global Investments reported a hacking incident, Yonhap reported. In Japan, hackers on Tuesday threatened to release data of traders using a GMO Internet Group cloud service for foreign-exchange trading. — Bloomberg

Bitcoin had dropped 4.5 per cent in 24 hours to $76,664 by 6am UAE time on Friday, crypto news website The Block reported. Ether fell 5.2 per cent to $2,190, while BNB, the token linked to Binance, slid 7.1 per cent to $698.65. He referred to Binance’s $144 billion in assets under custody and the speed with which stablecoin issuers froze funds. Separately, prediction market Polymarket briefly halted trading on Thursday after users reported unauthorised withdrawals linked to a compromised third-party provider.

extraction.body: Binance halted trading Thursday after hackers allegedly linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion, the largest crypto hack in history. Why it matters : The attack comes after a wave of high-profile cyber intrusions and data breaches during "Black October," when a series of security incidents and AI -discovered bugs triggered fears of a global crisis. Driving the news: Binance co-founder Yi He said on X that the crypto exchange had suspended deposits and withdrawals. "User funds are safe," she wrote. "Binance will cover all hacking losses." An estimated $6.3 billion were drained from wallets in the incident, Binance said , although the exchange and partners managed to freeze about $3 billion that can potentially be recovered. "This is unprecedented," said Kevin March, a co-founder of JPEG Trading, a cryptocurrency trading firm that closely tracked the hack to monitor market conditions. An initial investigation linked the hack to a compromised laptop from one Binance engineer. That access allowed an attacker to gain access to Binance's systems to make withdrawals, the exchange said. Zoom in: Researchers from TRM Labs and Pangolin Intelligence found that the attack appeared to be the work of a North Korean hacking collective. "This was absolutely North Korea," Nick Carlsen, a senior TRM investigator, told the Wall Street Journal . Representatives of North Korea have previously denied allegations of hacking crypto exchanges. The country has turned hacking and scams into an industrial-scale scourge, focusing on crypto heists and a widespread practice of tricking Western companies into hiring North Korean workers . A Binance spokesperson said the exchange's security teams are "reviewing all relevant information with urgency." The big picture: If estimates hold up, the Binance hack would be the biggest crypto attack in history. In 2025, North Korea-linked hackers stole about $1.5 billion worth of crypto from the Bybit exchange. Between the lines: Crypto is a relatively common hacking target, but massive attacks can leave smaller exchanges vulnerable to collapse due to the potential for panicked withdrawals. Binance's size makes it more insulated, March said. "If this happened to any other business in crypto other than Binance, it would've been catastrophic." The exchange is capable of covering potential losses through its insurance and balance sheet, he said, although broad reverberations in crypto markets and prices remain possible. The intrigue: Reports of a breach came just hours after Polymarket confirmed it was facing a cyberattack, prompting the decentralized prediction market operator to pause trading for an hour after an attacker made off with at least $2.7 million in user funds. Researchers at Hudson Rock tied the Polymarket incident to a breach involving third-party website monitoring tool DebugBear , which said earlier Thursday it was responding to its own security incident. What to watch: Binance has yet to confirm who may be behind the attack and the total value of the currencies suspected hackers made off with. extraction.body: Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, said $6.3 billion of funds are involved in what the industry is describing as crypto’s biggest-ever hack. Digital tokens fell. “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said in a post on X. “We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far.” Binance has temporarily suspended all withdrawals, which it expects to resume within 48 hours, co-founder Yi He said in a post on X. The company said it will cover all losses and “user funds are safe.” Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs said North Korea was behind the heist, which it called “the largest crypto theft on record.” “TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” the firm said. “We make this judgment with high confidence.” Before now, the biggest publicly known crypto hack occurred at exchange Bybit in February 2025, in which attackers made off with almost $1.5 billion of tokens. For crypto faithful who’d been basking in a two-month-long price rebound, the Binance incident is a potential setback. Notorious previous episodes of theft and fraud among fallen crypto giants such as FTX and Mt. Gox set the stage for protracted bear markets, bruises the industry has worked to put behind it in US President Donald Trump’s promised new era of regulatory clarity for cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin dropped 3% at the end of the US session and a further 3% in Asia trading, falling below $77,000 to its lowest level since September, with other tokens also selling off. “The rumored Binance hack is definitely driving down coin prices,” said Fredrick Collins, chief executive and co-founder of crypto data platform Velo Data. “Binance is such a behemoth in crypto that any hit to confidence in them is a hit to confidence in the industry as a whole, especially as people have already been skittish over the increasing cyber capabilities of AI.” The hackers appear to have exploited how Binance authorizes transactions, according to TRM. They seemingly gained access to the exchange’s systems and used internal software to authorize transfers across 10 different blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, it said. Binance said the incident may involve a compromised software engineer’s laptop. “We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak,” the company said. An emergency insurance and reserve fund from Binance called the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) was established in 2018 to serve a backstop for customers in “extreme situations,” according to the exchange. The SAFU is generally maintained at around $1 billion, but has fluctuated in the past in tandem with market movements, Binance said in 2024. The two biggest stablecoin issuers said they took steps to freeze missing currency. Paolo Ardoino, the chief executive officer of Tether, said in an X post that it froze more than $1.5 billion of the stablecoin “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.” Jeremy Allaire, who runs Circle Internet Group Inc., said $800 million of its coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit involving Binance.” Sentiment was already fragile after a spate of crypto security incidents. In recent months, hundreds of millions of dollars were drained from Bitget, while tampering tied to Ledger devices also led to millions of dollars in losses. “Attackers are operating at unprecedented speed and scale” but “the tools to track and trace operate at that speed too,” said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “Stablecoin issuers freeze within hours. Investigators follow funds across chains in real time.” Traders had already been bracing for greater volatility in the crypto market this week, with $11 billion in options set to expire Friday. This comes days ahead of the US midterm elections taking place next week, when Democrats could potentially retake one or both chambers of Congress and open the door to greater regulatory scrutiny for the industry. Exchange thefts and malfeasance have been an ever-present backdrop of crypto’s almost two-decade ascent, the most famous of which was the collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX in November 2022. In what remains perhaps the most notorious hacking incident, Japan-based Bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was struck in 2011. Over time, the hackers made off with tokens worth billions of dollars based on the current market price. Mt. Gox eventually went bankrupt. “It’s a huge damage to crypto because of the consistent successful hacks in the space,” said Tian Zeng, chief executive officer of crypto hedge fund Third Eye. “The fact that exploits keep happening makes it dangerous in the age of newest AI models being released every two weeks.” The Binance incident came on the same day event-contract venue Polymarket halted trading on its international exchange for an hour after it said that a third-party software provider was compromised. More than 700 Polymarket users were drained of $2.7 million in funds, said blockchain analytics platform Bubblemaps, in a post on X. A spokesman declined to comment on the numbers. Recent security incidents haven’t been confined to crypto firms. South Korea’s Daishin Securities disclosed a data leak affecting about 38,000 customers this week, and Mirae Asset Global Investments reported a hacking incident, Yonhap reported. In Japan, hackers on Tuesday threatened to release data of traders using a GMO Internet Group cloud service for foreign-exchange trading. — Bloomberg

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency prices fell sharply after Binance , the world’s largest crypto exchange, disclosed a security breach that it estimates has affected about $6.3 billion in assets. Bitcoin had dropped 4.5 per cent in 24 hours to $76,664 by 6am UAE time on Friday, crypto news website The Block reported. Ether fell 5.2 per cent to $2,190, while BNB, the token linked to Binance, slid 7.1 per cent to $698.65. At 7.51am UAE time, Bitcoin was trading at $77,984, down 2.2 per cent over 24 hours, data platform CoinGecko found. Ether was down 3.2 per cent at $2,230 and BNB was 3.9 per cent lower at $716.69. More than $1.5 billion of leveraged positions were liquidated in 24 hours, most of them bets on rising prices, The Block reported, quoting CoinGlass data. “The Binance exploit has intensified market-wide selling, with BNB facing the greatest exposure,” Dominick John, an analyst at Zeus Research, told The Block . Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated the theft at about $5.9 billion at the time it happened, crypto news website CoinDesk reported. TRM Labs linked the attack with “high confidence” to North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor. About $3 billion has been frozen, including more than $2.3 billion in stablecoins. Binance co-chief executive Yi He said the exchange would cover all losses. Rick Maeda, head of markets at Laevitas, told The Block that BNB’s fall was “quite modest for possibly the largest exchange theft ever”. He referred to Binance’s $144 billion in assets under custody and the speed with which stablecoin issuers froze funds. Separately, prediction market Polymarket briefly halted trading on Thursday after users reported unauthorised withdrawals linked to a compromised third-party provider.

KAUA'I, Hawai'i (Island News) -- Kauaʻi police recovered a stolen truck in Līhuʻe with help from automated license plate reader technology. The truck was reported stolen on October 15. Detectives later learned its original license plates had been replaced with fake novelty plates. On October 29, the department’s license plate reader system detected the altered plate and alerted officers to the vehicle’s possible location. Detectives and patrol officers then worked together to find and recover the truck without incident. Police say the technology helped identify the vehicle, but does not identify the person driving it. After further investigation, officers identified 46-year-old Kysen Palmeira of Wailua as the suspect. Palmeira was arrested on suspicion of first-degree unauthorized control of a propelled vehicle and an outstanding bench warrant. Officers also seized a second vehicle as evidence after suspected narcotics were found. Do you have a story idea? Email news tips to news@kitv.com

LIHU‘E — The Kaua‘i Police Department (KPD) is introducing Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) technology as part of its ongoing efforts to enhance public safety, strengthen investigative capabilities, and improve the department’s ability to respond to criminal activity throughout the island. “The introduction of ALPR technology represents another step toward providing our officers with modern tools to better serve and protect our community,” said Chief of Police Rudy Tai. “Our goal is to use this technology responsibly to assist investigations, improve public safety, and help to keep Kaua‘i a safe place for our residents and visitors.” ALPR technology is a law enforcement tool that automatically captures and records license plate information from vehicles passing designated locations. The technology helps investigators identify vehicles potentially associated with criminal investigations, including stolen vehicles, missing persons, and other public safety incidents. Unlike traditional surveillance cameras, ALPR cameras are not designed to provide continuous live video monitoring of public areas. Instead, these specialized cameras capture license plate information and associated vehicle images, that authorized law enforcement personnel may use for legitimate law enforcement purposes. The implementation of this technology is intended to enhance existing investigative methods, allowing officers to identify vehicles of interest and develop investigative leads more efficiently. ALPR technology does not replace traditional police work but rather serves as an additional resource to support investigations and public safety operations. Additionally, KPD’s ALPR technology should not be confused with the Flock Safety camera ALPR technology, which is a private company that stores data on its own servers. Flock camera data is accessible to anyone with a subscription, whereas data collected by KPD’s ALPR cameras is only accessible within KPD. “KPD recognizes the importance of balancing public safety with individual privacy, and the department is committed to using the technology responsibly for legitimate law enforcement purposes,” Tai said. “Access to information collected through the ALPR system will be restricted to authorized KPD personnel and governed by departmental policies and applicable laws.” As new technologies are incorporated into its law enforcement operations, KPD remains committed to transparency, accountability, and maintaining the trust of its community.

ALPR technology is a law enforcement tool that automatically captures and records license plate information from vehicles passing designated locations. LIHU‘E — The Kaua‘i Police Department (KPD) is introducing Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) technology as part of its ongoing efforts to enhance public safety, strengthen investigative capabilities, and improve the department’s ability to respond to criminal activity throughout the island. “The introduction of ALPR technology represents another step toward providing our officers with modern tools to better serve and protect our community,” said Chief of Police Rudy Tai. “Our goal is to use this technology responsibly to assist investigations, improve public safety, and help to keep Kaua‘i a safe place for our residents and visitors.” ALPR technology is a law enforcement tool that automatically captures and records license plate information from vehicles passing designated locations. The technology helps investigators identify vehicles potentially associated with criminal investigations, including stolen vehicles, missing persons, and other public safety incidents. Unlike traditional surveillance cameras, ALPR cameras are not designed to provide continuous live video monitoring of public areas. Instead, these specialized cameras capture license plate information and associated vehicle images, that authorized law enforcement personnel may use for legitimate law enforcement purposes. The implementation of this technology is intended to enhance existing investigative methods, allowing officers to identify vehicles of interest and develop investigative leads more efficiently. ALPR technology does not replace traditional police work but rather serves as an additional resource to support investigations and public safety operations. Additionally, KPD’s ALPR technology should not be confused with the Flock Safety camera ALPR technology, which is a private company that stores data on its own servers. Flock camera data is accessible to anyone with a subscription, whereas data collected by KPD’s ALPR cameras is only accessible within KPD. “KPD recognizes the importance of balancing public safety with individual privacy, and the department is committed to using the technology responsibly for legitimate law enforcement purposes,” Tai said. “Access to information collected through the ALPR system will be restricted to authorized KPD personnel and governed by departmental policies and applicable laws.” As new technologies are incorporated into its law enforcement operations, KPD remains committed to transparency, accountability, and maintaining the trust of its community.

Flock camera data is accessible to anyone with a subscription, whereas data collected by KPD’s ALPR cameras is only accessible within KPD.

sources.title: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
passages: But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.) "“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”" - Derek Mulvey But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider.

“The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.” Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported.
Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028.

But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027.
Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year.
In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.
A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD.
And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.
Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed.
Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems.
To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo.

extraction.body: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe just made it clear where the company's real ambitions lie, and it's not just building electric SUVs. During last night's earnings call, Scaringe spent more time hyping the EV maker's unproven autonomous vehicle plans than discussing the production ramp of the crucial R2 SUV. The company is racing toward a critical milestone: rolling out point-to-point hands-free driving to employees later this year, with customer access coming in 2027 and a full robotaxi partnership with Uber launching in 2028. The next two years will determine whether Rivian can pull off one of the auto industry's riskiest pivots. Rivian is making a high-stakes bet that could redefine its future, and it's not about building more electric trucks. During an hourlong earnings call last night, CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time discussing the production ramp of the company's all-important R2 SUV and more time hyping the EV maker's still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions. While competitors like Tesla continue to dominate EV sales and traditional automakers ramp up electric offerings, Rivian is doubling down on self-driving technology as its differentiator. It's a gamble that could either vault the company ahead of rivals or distract from the core business of selling vehicles. Rivian faces its first real test later this year when it rolls out point-to-point hands-free driving to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026. Customer access won't arrive until 2027, giving Rivian a full year to work out the inevitable bugs and edge cases that plague autonomous systems. But the real moonshot comes in 2028, when Rivian plans to launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber. The deal positions Rivian to compete directly with Waymo, Cruise, and Tesla's own robotaxi ambitions. Uber's recent company-wide rollout of ChatGPT signals the ride-hailing giant's broader AI push, making Rivian a natural partner for autonomous vehicle deployment. The timeline is aggressive, especially for a company that's still struggling to achieve profitability on its existing vehicle lineup. Rivian has been burning through cash while ramping production of its R1T truck and R1S SUV, and the R2 was supposed to be the more affordable model that would finally bring the company to sustainable scale. Now Scaringe is essentially telling investors that autonomy, not volume production, is where Rivian's future lies. Tesla has been promising full self-driving capability for years, but regulatory scrutiny continues to mount. The NHTSA recently launched a probe into Tesla's robotaxis for allegedly speeding in school zones, while the company was forced to drop the "Full Self-Driving" name in Europe after regulators called it misleading. Rivian's autonomy push builds on the company's AI and self-driving technology showcase from earlier this year, where it detailed its sensor suite, custom chips, and software stack. The company is betting that its ground-up approach to autonomous vehicles, rather than retrofitting existing platforms, will give it an edge. The shift also comes as the broader auto industry grapples with the enormous capital requirements of developing self-driving technology. Doug Field, who recently joined Rivian spinoff Mind Robotics as chief, brings deep expertise from his time leading Ford's EV efforts and architecting Tesla's Model 3, but the challenges remain immense. For Rivian, the next two years represent a make-or-break period. The company must execute flawlessly on its employee testing program, gather enough real-world data to validate safety claims, navigate a complex regulatory environment, and convince customers that its autonomous technology is ready for prime time. While Waymo operates commercial services in limited markets, no company has yet demonstrated the ability to run profitable, city-wide autonomous ride-hailing operations. Rivian is betting it can crack that code by 2028, a timeline that leaves little room for delays or setbacks. Investors will be watching closely to see whether Scaringe's autonomy-first messaging translates into tangible progress. The company's willingness to prioritize self-driving development over near-term production targets suggests confidence in its technology roadmap, but it also raises questions about whether Rivian is spreading itself too thin. Building a successful car company is hard enough without simultaneously trying to solve one of the auto industry's most complex technical challenges. Rivian's aggressive push into autonomy represents one of the boldest strategic pivots in the EV industry. By prioritizing self-driving technology over production volume, Scaringe is making a calculated bet that robotaxis and advanced driver assistance will define the next decade of transportation. But with employee testing starting in just months and a full robotaxi launch scheduled for 2028, the execution window is razor-thin. If Rivian can deliver on its autonomous promises while keeping its core EV business afloat, it could emerge as a major player in the self-driving revolution. If not, the company risks becoming a cautionary tale about overextending in pursuit of moonshots.

extraction.body: During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions. But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player. “We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.) "“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”" - Derek Mulvey But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse. Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.” Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin. Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong. To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

extraction.body: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe just made it clear where the company's real ambitions lie, and it's not just building electric SUVs. During last night's earnings call, Scaringe spent more time hyping the EV maker's unproven autonomous vehicle plans than discussing the production ramp of the crucial R2 SUV. The company is racing toward a critical milestone: rolling out point-to-point hands-free driving to employees later this year, with customer access coming in 2027 and a full robotaxi partnership with Uber launching in 2028. The next two years will determine whether Rivian can pull off one of the auto industry's riskiest pivots. Rivian is making a high-stakes bet that could redefine its future, and it's not about building more electric trucks. During an hourlong earnings call last night, CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time discussing the production ramp of the company's all-important R2 SUV and more time hyping the EV maker's still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions. While competitors like Tesla continue to dominate EV sales and traditional automakers ramp up electric offerings, Rivian is doubling down on self-driving technology as its differentiator. It's a gamble that could either vault the company ahead of rivals or distract from the core business of selling vehicles. Rivian faces its first real test later this year when it rolls out point-to-point hands-free driving to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026. Customer access won't arrive until 2027, giving Rivian a full year to work out the inevitable bugs and edge cases that plague autonomous systems. But the real moonshot comes in 2028, when Rivian plans to launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber. The deal positions Rivian to compete directly with Waymo, Cruise, and Tesla's own robotaxi ambitions. Uber's recent company-wide rollout of ChatGPT signals the ride-hailing giant's broader AI push, making Rivian a natural partner for autonomous vehicle deployment. The timeline is aggressive, especially for a company that's still struggling to achieve profitability on its existing vehicle lineup. Rivian has been burning through cash while ramping production of its R1T truck and R1S SUV, and the R2 was supposed to be the more affordable model that would finally bring the company to sustainable scale. Now Scaringe is essentially telling investors that autonomy, not volume production, is where Rivian's future lies. Tesla has been promising full self-driving capability for years, but regulatory scrutiny continues to mount. The NHTSA recently launched a probe into Tesla's robotaxis for allegedly speeding in school zones, while the company was forced to drop the "Full Self-Driving" name in Europe after regulators called it misleading. Rivian's autonomy push builds on the company's AI and self-driving technology showcase from earlier this year, where it detailed its sensor suite, custom chips, and software stack. The company is betting that its ground-up approach to autonomous vehicles, rather than retrofitting existing platforms, will give it an edge. The shift also comes as the broader auto industry grapples with the enormous capital requirements of developing self-driving technology. Doug Field, who recently joined Rivian spinoff Mind Robotics as chief, brings deep expertise from his time leading Ford's EV efforts and architecting Tesla's Model 3, but the challenges remain immense. For Rivian, the next two years represent a make-or-break period. The company must execute flawlessly on its employee testing program, gather enough real-world data to validate safety claims, navigate a complex regulatory environment, and convince customers that its autonomous technology is ready for prime time. While Waymo operates commercial services in limited markets, no company has yet demonstrated the ability to run profitable, city-wide autonomous ride-hailing operations. Rivian is betting it can crack that code by 2028, a timeline that leaves little room for delays or setbacks. Investors will be watching closely to see whether Scaringe's autonomy-first messaging translates into tangible progress. The company's willingness to prioritize self-driving development over near-term production targets suggests confidence in its technology roadmap, but it also raises questions about whether Rivian is spreading itself too thin. Building a successful car company is hard enough without simultaneously trying to solve one of the auto industry's most complex technical challenges. Rivian's aggressive push into autonomy represents one of the boldest strategic pivots in the EV industry. By prioritizing self-driving technology over production volume, Scaringe is making a calculated bet that robotaxis and advanced driver assistance will define the next decade of transportation. But with employee testing starting in just months and a full robotaxi launch scheduled for 2028, the execution window is razor-thin. If Rivian can deliver on its autonomous promises while keeping its core EV business afloat, it could emerge as a major player in the self-driving revolution. If not, the company risks becoming a cautionary tale about overextending in pursuit of moonshots.

extraction.body: Binance's estimated $6.3 billion hack is drawing scrutiny beyond the cryptocurrency industry, with security experts warning that trusted devices and legitimate credentials can give criminals a route into systems without stealing the cryptographic keys that protect digital assets. The exchange initially said a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals. It reported finding no evidence of a wallet private key leak. "We don't know the full details of this incident yet, and we may not for some time," Tomas Sinicki, managing director at Coveron, an identity theft and scam protection service developed by Nord Security, told IBT. "But even what is confirmed so far points to a familiar pattern." Binance subsequently disclosed additional breach points. Co-CEO Richard Teng said the attack involved a more complex process than simply using one engineer's permissions, cautioning against attributing responsibility to an individual. Frances Zelazny, general manager of new market initiatives at Prove, told IBT that the distinction between a trusted device and a trustworthy action is central to understanding the risks. "Securing a credential is not the same as securing the identity and authority behind an action," she said. "A device is not a person. An employee's legitimate device can be compromised." "A credential is not a person either, especially in a world where credentials are not bound to humans and can be used by someone or something else." Binance said approximately $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen and pledged to cover losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, and company resources. On Friday, CoinDesk reported that the exchange had set aside more than $6.34 billion, separate from frozen assets, to address the losses. However, reimbursement does not resolve the security questions raised by the intrusion. "At the same time, authentication does not equate to authorization," Zelazny said. "A legitimate user or service may have access it should not have." "And a digital signature does not establish intent. It establishes that the required cryptographic authorization occurred, not that the transaction or the person behind it was legitimate." Her warning addresses the possibility that an attacker could manipulate an authorized system while the underlying cryptographic safeguards continue functioning. "The lesson from Binance is not that cryptography failed," Zelazny said. "It's that protecting keys may not be enough if the systems authorized to use them can be manipulated." Binance has promised a detailed technical account after investigators verify the facts. The final losses, recovery totals and full intrusion path remain unsettled. "Much of this story is still uncertain: the final losses, the number of breach points, even who is responsible," Sinicki said. "That uncertainty is a lesson in itself: by the time the facts are settled, the damage is done." He warned that smaller victims lack comparable recovery resources. "This is something we see at the individual level too, having supported customers through crypto wallet wipeouts that they could not reverse on their own," Sinicki said. Zelazny questioned how a less financially resilient organization would survive."What happens next time, when the organization on the other side of the attack cannot absorb billions in losses?" she asked. For Sinicki, the priority is prevention: "When identity is the entry point, protection has to come before the breach, not after."

sources.title: North Korean hackers steal $6.3B from Binance in ‘largest bank heist in human history’ - New York Post
passages: North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.”

State-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor was formed around 2016 and tasked with stealing cryptocurrency, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 nations including the US that tracks North Korean sanctions violations.
A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI.
US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program.
Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news.
Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion.
Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m.
ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders.
Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets.
Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop.

In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person.
Binance maintains a $1 billion bitcoin reserve asset fund for users designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet.
“We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
The culprits targeted just a few accounts, including one crypto wallet holding nearly $800 million, Idan Ofrat, co-founder of Fireblocks, told The Post.

Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West.

“We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said, noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
Chainalysis co-founder Jonathan Levin also suspected North Korean hackers, writing that they “are up to their old tricks.”
A massive $1.5 billion heist targeting crypto exchange Bybit last year was also pinned on the North Korean cybercrime group, given the code name TraderTraitor by the FBI.
Last month, North Korean groups were suspected in the theft of over $350 million in crypto in a hack of crypto exchange Bitget.

While the loss is severe and marks a record theft for the industry, it’s still just a fraction of Binance’s total balance sheet. The exchange holds a total of $167 billion in crypto assets across its digital wallets, according to blockchain analytics firm Nansen.

North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a lightning-fast theft that an insider has called “the largest bank heist in human history.”

Cybercriminals swiped the digital coins out of Binance wallets within a mere 20 minutes starting at 4:30 p.m. ET Thursday, exploiting the system by hacking into an engineer’s laptop, according to analytics firm TRM Labs and industry insiders.

Binance initially said the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop. In an update Friday, Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s security team has “uncovered additional points of breach,” suggesting it was a complex attack carried out by more than one person.
The culprits targeted just a few accounts, including one crypto wallet holding nearly $800 million, Idan Ofrat, co-founder of Fireblocks, told The Post.

TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of the crime, is known for pulling off unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover. US officials have said cybercrime attacks fund roughly half of North Korea’s missile program.

Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms.

The crypto exchange added that it’s on track to allow customers to make withdrawals within two days and that it has set over $6 billion of company funds aside to cover customers’ losses. It suspended withdrawals and vowed to cover all losses immediately after the attack.
Meanwhile, co-CEO Changpeng Zhao tried to stop Tesla and SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk from adding to the chaos online, telling him that it’s a “bad time to troll.”

Musk posted several laughing- and grimacing-face emojis on X, his social-media platform, reacting to the news. Zhao responded by reminding Musk that Binance holds a stake in his businesses worth more than $1 billion.

“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop,” Zhao wrote. “Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!”

Bitcoin dropped below $80,000 for the first time in a month, ether fell to a two-month low of $2,230 and crypto-related stocks plummeted as the hack served as a stunning reminder that the crypto industry still remains a largely unregulated Wild West.

She said she has concerns about Election Day but believes voter apathy poses a threat as well. "I do think we are going to see problems," Grant said. "We can't just keep on saying my votes not going to county, we gotta say we gotta do it and see what the outcome is," she added. City officials are taking steps to protect the voting process and its outcome. The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office announced that its Election Task Force will be mobilized Tuesday, an effort officials have been planning since the summer. Fifty assistant district attorneys will be deployed to respond to issues, and a hotline will be available for anyone who witnesses problems. "Our main role on Election Day is to make sure everyone gets a chance to vote. We are not looking to do anything other than make things run smooth," Assistant District Attorney Brian Collins said. The Department of Justice also plans to send federal election monitors to Philadelphia. Officials said they are not concerned about the move because it has been done in the past. Some voters said they welcome the increased security. "I just think that with all the hype and everything that's happened. I think whoever the poll watchers are they are more aware of that," said Tyrone Wrice of West Philadelphia. Others said they wanted to make sure they voted early. "I did have a slight concern. Thats why i came to city hall and hand out my ballot to make sure it got in there," said Colleen Chambers of Northern Liberties. Wrice emphasized the importance of casting a ballot. "The power of the vote, even though it's one, is probably the most powerful thing we have," he said. The Election Task Force will remain activated until every vote is counted. Voters in Pennsylvania who are in line by 8 p.m. cannot be turned away.

extraction.body: Quanda Grant, of West Philadelphia, was outside City Hall on her way to drop off her mail-in ballot. She said she has concerns about Election Day but believes voter apathy poses a threat as well. "I do think we are going to see problems," Grant said. "We can't just keep on saying my votes not going to county, we gotta say we gotta do it and see what the outcome is," she added. City officials are taking steps to protect the voting process and its outcome. The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office announced that its Election Task Force will be mobilized Tuesday, an effort officials have been planning since the summer. Fifty assistant district attorneys will be deployed to respond to issues, and a hotline will be available for anyone who witnesses problems. "Our main role on Election Day is to make sure everyone gets a chance to vote. We are not looking to do anything other than make things run smooth," Assistant District Attorney Brian Collins said. The Department of Justice also plans to send federal election monitors to Philadelphia. Officials said they are not concerned about the move because it has been done in the past. Some voters said they welcome the increased security. "I just think that with all the hype and everything that's happened. I think whoever the poll watchers are they are more aware of that," said Tyrone Wrice of West Philadelphia. Others said they wanted to make sure they voted early. "I did have a slight concern. Thats why i came to city hall and hand out my ballot to make sure it got in there," said Colleen Chambers of Northern Liberties. Wrice emphasized the importance of casting a ballot. "The power of the vote, even though it's one, is probably the most powerful thing we have," he said. The Election Task Force will remain activated until every vote is counted. Voters in Pennsylvania who are in line by 8 p.m. cannot be turned away.

So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean.
Binance is the world's biggest, which is part of what makes the hack so monumental.
While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin.

extraction.body: From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance , the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines. The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves. These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand. So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean. While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it? Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions. This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers. Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam" . Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets. In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes. In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump. Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto. Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name. Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes. The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain. A crypto exchange is the digital platform where investors can buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies. Similar to traditional investing, a crypto exchange acts as a brokerage where people can transfer traditional money, like pounds or dollars, in exchange for cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or Ethereum. Most transactions are accompanied by fees. Binance is the world's biggest, which is part of what makes the hack so monumental. A crypto wallet is a place where investors hold their cryptocurrency. There are two types, a hot wallet and a cold wallet. Cold wallets are physical devices like specially designed USB sticks that store crypto offline typically for safer and longer term storage. Ethereum is used to describe both the second largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, represented by the Ether token, and the blockchain underpinning it. This supports an array of different applications and digital assets, such as non-fungible tokens. It functions in a similar way to Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, but in 2022 switched to a greener operating system requiring less computers and energy . ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies. A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day. While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges. Meme coins are a form of cryptocurrency used for fun and speculation. But meme coins are heavily criticised for their speculative nature and the risk involved for investors, as they often have little prospect of accumulating value over time. They can also be susceptible to "rug pulls" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers to raise the price of their coin, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales. Some celebrities have faced backlash after launching meme coins. Stablecoins themselves are usually controlled by companies that provide them, with transactions recorded on digital ledgers. While held up by some as the future of finance, high profile price collapses of stablecoins have alerted regulators to risks for investors and prompted scrutiny over their supposed stability. XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation. Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain. This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value . The BBC's Lucy Woodham explains why a blue donkey and a red elephant are used in US politics. The murderer of Colleen Slemmer is said to be walking and talking in limited ways after two doses of lethal injection.

extraction.body: From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance , the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines. The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves. These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand. So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean. While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it? Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions. This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers. Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam" . Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets. In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes. In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump. Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto. Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name. Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes. The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain. A crypto exchange is the digital platform where investors can buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies. Similar to traditional investing, a crypto exchange acts as a brokerage where people can transfer traditional money, like pounds or dollars, in exchange for cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or Ethereum. Most transactions are accompanied by fees. Binance is the world's biggest, which is part of what makes the hack so monumental. A crypto wallet is a place where investors hold their cryptocurrency. There are two types, a hot wallet and a cold wallet. Cold wallets are physical devices like specially designed USB sticks that store crypto offline typically for safer and longer term storage. Ethereum is used to describe both the second largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, represented by the Ether token, and the blockchain underpinning it. This supports an array of different applications and digital assets, such as non-fungible tokens. It functions in a similar way to Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, but in 2022 switched to a greener operating system requiring less computers and energy . ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies. A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day. While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges. Meme coins are a form of cryptocurrency used for fun and speculation. But meme coins are heavily criticised for their speculative nature and the risk involved for investors, as they often have little prospect of accumulating value over time. They can also be susceptible to "rug pulls" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers to raise the price of their coin, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales. Some celebrities have faced backlash after launching meme coins. Stablecoins themselves are usually controlled by companies that provide them, with transactions recorded on digital ledgers. While held up by some as the future of finance, high profile price collapses of stablecoins have alerted regulators to risks for investors and prompted scrutiny over their supposed stability. XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation. Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain. This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value . The BBC's Lucy Woodham explains why a blue donkey and a red elephant are used in US politics. The murderer of Colleen Slemmer is said to be walking and talking in limited ways after two doses of lethal injection.

extraction.body: Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers. On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea. The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day. By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital. The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC. "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network." Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble. In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data. More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets. What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. "The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC. Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted. Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point. "We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options." GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin. "Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC. The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day. Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment. Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said. "Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. "The current holder base is a pretty strong one that is able to look at these things with a slightly longer-term view. That's playing a big role in how bitcoin is behaving well in this negative market environment." extraction.body: Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers. On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea. The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day. By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital. The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC. "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network." Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble. In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data. More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets. What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. "The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC. Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted. Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point. "We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options." GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin. "Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC. The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day. Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment. Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said. "Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. "The current holder base is a pretty strong one that is able to look at these things with a slightly longer-term view. That's playing a big role in how bitcoin is behaving well in this negative market environment." sources.title: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
passages: Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively.
Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s.
After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work.
The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment.
Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor.
Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.

The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit.

Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.

The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications. After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite. A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally. The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools. Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation. If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links. Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively.
